t.al zubarah archaeological site@26.0,51.0:
Out on the north-west coast of Qatar, where the desert slides into a shallow turquoise sea, stand the low ruins of Al Zubarah, once one of the busiest pearling and trading towns in the Gulf. In the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries the town thrived on pearls dived from the oyster beds offshore, traded on to India, Persia and beyond. Then it declined, was abandoned in the early twentieth century, and the sand covered it. Archaeologists have since uncovered streets, houses, a souk, mosques and a long town wall running in an arc around the old harbour. UNESCO inscribed the site in 2013.

The most visible building is not part of the old town at all. Al Zubarah Fort, a square, sand-coloured structure with round and square corner towers, was built in the 1930s as a coastguard post and now houses exhibits on the history of the area. Climb its walls and you look across a flat landscape of scrub and salt, with the sea beyond and, on a clear day, a sense of how close Bahrain is across the water.

The ride here is about space and light. Good, wide roads run north from Doha through open desert, straight for long distances and largely empty once you leave the city's outer suburbs. That sounds dull, and partly it is, but the emptiness has its own appeal: dunes and low ridges, camels grazing by the road, farms with patches of green, and the strange sight of mirages trembling over the tarmac. Watch for sand blowing across the road, especially in the afternoon when the wind picks up, and for camels, which wander freely and are very big.

Heat is the defining condition. From late spring to early autumn temperatures easily climb past forty degrees, with high humidity near the coast, and riding in the middle of the day is genuinely dangerous. Go in winter, roughly November to March, when mornings are pleasant and evenings cool.

There is nothing at the site in the way of fuel, and only limited facilities. The nearest town is Madinat ash Shamal, about twenty-four kilometres away, with fuel and shops. Carry plenty of water, keep a full tank and plan your day around the early morning and late afternoon light, when the ruins glow gold against the sea.
t.hayr shtayyah@26.6,50.8:
Hayr Shtayyah is not a place you can ride to. It is an oyster bed lying in the open sea off the northeast coast of Bahrain, one of three offshore pearl beds included in the UNESCO site Pearling, Testimony of an Island Economy, listed in 2012. For centuries, pearling was the backbone of Bahrain's economy: every summer, fleets of wooden dhows sailed out to the banks, and divers plunged repeatedly into the warm water with a nose clip, a stone weight and a basket, holding their breath for minutes to gather oysters. Then the Japanese cultured pearl and the arrival of oil in the 1930s brought the industry to an end almost overnight.

The onshore part of the UNESCO site is where you can actually go, in the old town of Muharraq. The Pearling Path is a walking route through narrow lanes, linking merchants' houses, traditional buildings and a museum that tells the story of the divers, the boat captains and the traders who grew rich from the trade. At the southern tip of Muharraq, the small Bu Mahir fort stands on the seashore where the pearling boats used to set off, and from there the path begins. The old houses, with their wind towers and carved wooden doors, are beautifully restored.

Riding in Bahrain is straightforward but not especially exciting. The country is small and flat, with good roads, modern highways and causeways linking the islands. Traffic around Manama and Muharraq is heavy at rush hour, and drivers can be impatient. The heat and humidity in summer are intense, with temperatures often above forty degrees, so ride early or late, and consider visiting in the cooler months from November to March. The long causeway to Saudi Arabia, the King Fahd Causeway, is an experience in itself, if you have the right paperwork.

Fuel is plentiful and cheap, and services are everywhere in Manama and Muharraq. Try machboos, spiced rice with chicken or fish, and halwa, a sticky sweet flavoured with saffron and rosewater, best with a cup of cardamom coffee. Look out to sea from the shore and imagine the white sails of the pearling fleet on the horizon.
t.madinat hamad 3 burial mound field@26.1,:
Bahrain was once covered with burial mounds. Over thousands of years, between roughly 2200 BC and the early centuries AD, the people of Dilmun, an ancient civilisation that controlled trade in the Gulf between Mesopotamia and the Indus valley, built tens of thousands of tombs across the northern part of the island. Many have been lost to modern development, but some fields survive, and in 2019 a selection of them, including the Madinat Hamad mound fields, was inscribed as the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Dilmun Burial Mounds.

The mounds are low, rounded heaps of stone and earth, some small, others large royal tombs, and they cluster together in fields on the gravelly plain. Each covered a stone chamber where the dead were buried with pottery, seals and other objects, many now in the Bahrain National Museum. The density of the mounds is remarkable, suggesting a large population and a culture deeply concerned with death and the afterlife. Dilmun was described in Mesopotamian texts as a land of paradise, and some scholars have linked it to the Garden of Eden.

Riding in Bahrain means dealing with busy multi-lane highways, fast traffic and roundabouts, and the island is small, so distances are short. The landscape is flat, with desert, towns and the sea never far away. Heat is the main challenge: from May to September, temperatures often exceed forty degrees, with high humidity, so riding is best in the early morning or in the cooler months from November to March. Dust and wind can reduce visibility. Driving is on the right, and speed cameras are common.

The mound field lies close to the towns of Dar Kulayb and Madinat Hamad, which have fuel, shops and restaurants. Fuel in Bahrain is cheap. Manama, the capital, is about twenty kilometres north, with all services and the Qal'at al-Bahrain, an ancient harbour and Portuguese fort, also a World Heritage Site. Food in Bahrain includes machboos, spiced rice with meat or fish, and fresh dates. Visiting the mounds at sunset, when the light turns gold and the heat begins to ease, is a memorable experience.
t.segment desaguadero titijoni@-16.5,-69.0:
At around 3,800 metres above sea level the air on the Altiplano is thin enough to make lacing your boots feel like exercise, and Desaguadero is a place where you should take everything at half speed. The town sits on the border between Peru and Bolivia at the southern end of Lake Titicaca, where the Desaguadero river drains the lake toward the south. The segment of old road near Titijoni is part of the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road network listed by UNESCO in 2014, which ran along the shores of Titicaca on its way between Cusco and the southern provinces.

Desaguadero itself is famous mainly as a border crossing and market town, crowded, noisy and full of trade, with vendors, minibuses and trucks squeezing through narrow streets on market days. Crossing between countries here can be slow and paperwork-heavy, so have your documents ready and patience in good supply. The Inca trace, by contrast, lies out in the quiet country beyond town, a line across fields and grassland among adobe farmsteads and grazing llamas and sheep.

The riding on the Altiplano is about altitude, wind and light rather than corners. Roads are long and straight across the plateau, with the lake glittering in the distance and the snow-capped Cordillera Real rising on the Bolivian side. The surface on main routes is mostly paved but can have potholes, speed bumps in villages and wandering animals. Afternoon wind can be strong and cold, nights freeze for much of the year, and the sun at this height burns exposed skin in minutes. Your engine will feel down on power, and so will you.

Desaguadero has fuel, food and basic lodging, though quality varies, and Yunguyo and Puno on the Peruvian side offer more choice. Across the border, the ancient site of Tiwanaku lies about thirty-six kilometres away, one of the great pre-Inca centres of the Andes, and well worth the detour if your papers allow it.

This is Aymara country, with a strong culture of markets, festivals and traditional dress, and a deep relationship with the lake. Drink plenty of water, eat something warm, perhaps trout from Titicaca, and take a moment by the old road to feel how big and how high this land really is.
t.segment juli cruz pata ccaje@-16.2,-69.4:
Juli sits on the south-western shore of Lake Titicaca at close to 3,900 metres, and the air is so thin and clear that the far side of the lake, in Bolivia, seems close enough to touch. The town is nicknamed the Rome of the Americas for its cluster of colonial churches, built by Dominican and Jesuit missionaries in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, with carved stone façades and dim interiors full of paintings. Just outside town, the segment of Inca road between Juli and Cruz Pata Ccaje is part of the Qhapaq Ñan, the Andean road system inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2014. This route, the Urcosuyu branch, ran along the lake towards what is now Bolivia.

The landscape is the altiplano: wide, open, with stone-walled fields, adobe farmhouses, herds of llamas and alpacas, and the deep blue of the lake always at the edge of vision. The people here are mostly Aymara, and the markets are full of women in bowler hats and colourful layered skirts selling potatoes, chuño, the freeze-dried potato of the Andes, and fish from the lake.

The main road, PE-3S, runs from Puno along the lake to Juli and on to the Bolivian border at Desaguadero. It is paved and mostly straight or gently curving, but the altitude affects everything: your body, your engine's power and your judgement. Take a few days to acclimatise before riding hard here. The wind can be strong and cold, especially in the afternoon, and the sun burns quickly. The dry season, from May to October, has clear skies and cold nights, sometimes below freezing; the wet season brings afternoon storms.

Traffic is moderate, with buses, trucks, minibuses and tricycle taxis. Watch out for animals on the road, especially near villages, and for speed bumps, which are frequent and sometimes unmarked.

Juli has fuel, small hotels and simple restaurants, and Ilave, thirty kilometres away, is a larger market town. Try trucha, trout from the lake, fried or grilled, and a hot mate de coca, the coca leaf tea that locals swear helps with the altitude. Sunset over the lake from one of Juli's hills, with the churches glowing gold, is not something you forget.
t.siyadi house@26.3,50.6:
Muharraq was Bahrain's capital before Manama took over, and it is still the island's most atmospheric old town, a tangle of narrow lanes, coral-stone houses and wind towers beside a shallow sea. Siyadi House belongs to a group of merchant houses built when pearls made Bahrain rich, and it stands in the middle of the Pearling Path, a UNESCO-listed route through the old town that traces the pearl trade from the oyster beds to the merchants' counting rooms. Carved wooden doors, plaster work and a tall wind tower that once caught the breeze are the signature of the house.

Before oil, pearls were the island's fortune. Boats left each summer for the oyster banks, divers working with a nose clip and a weighted rope, and the merchants who bought the catch lived in houses like this one. The trade collapsed in the early twentieth century when cultured pearls from Japan flooded the market, and the later finding of oil in the 1930s changed Bahrain's course. The old merchant houses fell into disrepair until restoration brought them back, and some are now museums or cultural centres.

The riding here is urban and hot. Muharraq is linked by causeways to Manama and the rest of the island, and the roads are good, with plenty of traffic, roundabouts and fast dual carriageways. The lanes of the old town are narrow, and a motorcycle is an easy way to explore them, though signs and one-way streets may confuse you. Summer is extremely hot and humid, with temperatures above forty degrees, so ride in the early morning or evening, or choose the cooler months from November to March. The sea breeze is welcome, but dust storms occasionally drift in from the desert.

Fuel is plentiful and inexpensive across Bahrain, and Muharraq has stations on its main roads, so there is no need to plan ahead. Food in the old town includes fish, rice dishes spiced with saffron, dates and halwa, a sticky sweet made with starch, sugar and nuts, and cafés serve strong cardamom coffee. Walk the Pearling Path on foot, preferably in the morning, and leave time for the seafront, where fishing dhows bob in the harbour.
t.madinat hamad 2 burial mound field@26.1,:
Flat, pale and apparently empty, the central plain of Bahrain hides one of the oldest cemeteries on earth. Some four thousand years ago the island of Dilmun, as it was known to the Sumerians, buried its dead under thousands upon thousands of low stone mounds, and in places like Madinat Hamad and A'ali the mounds still stand in dense, grey fields. At one time there may have been several hundred thousand of them, which would have made Dilmun a famous necropolis in its day, and many have since been flattened by roads, housing and quarrying.

Madinat Hamad itself is a modern town, built in the late twentieth century as a planned suburb, and the contrast is sharp: new villas and roundabouts on one side of a road, ancient burial mounds a short walk away. Some of the mounds have been excavated, revealing stone chambers with the remains of the dead and grave goods such as pottery and beads. Others are still intact, and the best you can do is walk carefully around the edge, read the signs, and notice how many humps stretch toward the horizon. Dilmun was a trading centre between Mesopotamia and the Indus valley, and it appears in the ancient story of Gilgamesh as a place of immortality.

Riding in Bahrain is easy, if hot. The roads are paved and well marked, with fast dual carriageways, many roundabouts and drivers who do not always signal. The land is flat, so wind and sun are the main hazards, and between June and September the heat is intense, with humidity from the Gulf adding to the discomfort. The cooler season from November to March is much kinder, with clear skies and mild temperatures. At the mounds, bring water, a hat and sunglasses, and stay on tracks, since the ground is uneven and the site is fragile.

Fuel is available throughout Madinat Hamad, which is large enough for stations, supermarkets and cafés, and fuel in Bahrain is cheap by European standards. If you want to see more of the island's older layers, the Dilmun temple at Barbar and the lone Tree of Life, a mesquite that stands in the desert near Jebel Dukhan, make good additions. Respect the mounds as graves and keep bikes off them.
t.hayr bu amamah@26.8,50.8:
Before oil, the Gulf lived on pearls. For centuries the shallow waters off Bahrain and the nearby coasts were dotted with oyster beds, called hayr in Arabic, and every summer fleets of wooden dhows sailed out to dive for them, with men holding their breath, a peg on their nose and a stone to sink them. A good season could make a merchant rich, but a diver's life was hard, with debts, disease and danger from sharks. The pearls from this sea were prized from India to Europe, until the 1930s, when the Japanese learned to culture pearls and the old market collapsed.

Hayr Bū ʿAmāmah is one of these oyster banks, and it is part of the UNESCO listing of 2012, the Pearling Testimony, an Island Economy, which also includes the old merchants' houses in Muharraq and a stretch of waterfront. The oyster beds lie offshore, in water a few metres to a dozen deep, and nothing marks them but the sea and the experience of the captains who know them. I cannot say the exact position on the water, and the point is that this is a place you see from a boat, not from a bike.

The riding is on land, and it is easy. Bahrain is a small island linked to the mainland of Saudi Arabia by the King Fahd Causeway, and its roads are smooth, wide and well lit, with fast highways, roundabouts and a lot of traffic in the cities. Fuel is cheap and plentiful. Muharraq, the old pearling town, is a pleasure to walk, with narrow lanes, wind towers, courtyard houses and cafes where men play dominoes and drink tea with cardamom.

The best months run from November to March, when the days are warm and the sea breeze is mild. Summers are punishingly hot and humid, above forty degrees. Take a dhow trip if you can, and try the local dish of machboos, spiced rice with fish or lamb, and a glass of fresh juice from a street stall. Mind your documents at the causeway, since the border between the two countries has its own rules, with a visa, vehicle paperwork and insurance for riders.
t.hayr bu l thamah@26.8,50.9:
This is not a place you ride to. Hayr Bu Thamah is an oyster bed out in the Gulf, northeast of Bahrain's Muharraq island, and on a map it is a dot of open water with nothing around it. For centuries the pearl divers of the Gulf set out in wooden boats to beds like this, dropped over the side with a nose clip and a basket, and came up with oysters that made the region rich long before oil did. Bahrain's pearling heritage, including the oyster beds, the old merchant houses in Muharraq and a coastal fort, is listed by UNESCO as a testimony to that island economy.

Pearling was brutal work. Divers worked from the boats for months in the summer season, held their breath for a minute or more, and often ended in debt to the captains who financed the voyage. The trade collapsed in the twentieth century when the Japanese began culturing pearls, and the finding of oil in the 1930s gave the Gulf another way forward. The old song traditions of the pearl boats, the sea songs called fijiri, are still performed in Bahrain today and are worth hearing if you get the chance.

What you can ride is the shore and the island next to it. Muharraq, linked by causeways to Manama, has narrow streets, a restored pearling trail of old houses and a souk, and the riding is slow and urban with some traffic. Roads on the main island are flat and fast, with wide highways, roundabouts and a lot of heat. Winter, from November to March, is the pleasant season. In summer it is hot and humid, and a ride in the evening is much better than at noon.

Fuel is plentiful and generally cheap on the island, and the causeway to Saudi Arabia, the King Fahd Causeway, is a famous piece of engineering, though border formalities apply and you should check your documents and insurance well before planning to cross. If you are on the water, you can arrange boat trips from Muharraq to look at the area, though the beds are protected. Try a plate of machboos, the spiced rice with fish or lamb, and a cup of cardamom coffee while you think about the divers.
t.amarat ali rashed fakhro@26.3,50.6:
Muharraq was the capital of Bahrain before Manama took over, and it is the part of the country where the old pearl trade still shows in the buildings. For centuries, before cultured pearls and oil, Bahrain lived on pearls. Hundreds of boats left each summer for the oyster beds, men dived without equipment, holding their breath and wearing a nose clip, and merchants in Muharraq bought the catch and sold it on to dealers in Bombay and Paris. The wealth shaped the town, and UNESCO listed the Pearling Path, a group of merchants' houses, shops and fortifications, in 2012.

The house of Ali Rashed Fakhro is one of the merchant dwellings, or amarat, in the old town. These buildings are low and enclosed, with thick coral-stone walls and carved wooden doors, and inside are courtyards, wind towers and rooms for receiving guests and storing pearls. Coral stone was bound with gypsum plaster, and the surface is often decorated with geometric patterns. Rooms were arranged to catch the sea breeze in a hot, humid climate, and the layering of old and new structures tells the story of a family business over generations.

The town is a maze of narrow lanes that were never meant for cars, and the best way to see them is on foot. Muharraq is joined to Manama by causeways, only a few kilometres apart, so you can cross in minutes. The roads of Bahrain are well surfaced and clean, and the traffic is dense but orderly. The summer heat is intense and humid, and the best months are November to March. Fuel is cheap and available all across the island, and cafes in Muharraq serve strong coffee, cardamom tea and Bahraini halwa, a sweet jelly made with sugar, cornflour and spice.

If you ride out along the coast, you can follow the Pearling Path towards the fort of Bu Mahir, which stood at the tip of the island and watched the sea. The sea itself has changed, because land reclamation has pushed the shoreline back, but the sense of a trading culture remains strong. A short ride across the King Fahd Causeway leads to Saudi Arabia, though you should check border rules carefully before going.
t.bagh e eram@29.6,52.5:
Shiraz is the city of poets, roses and nightingales, and the Eram garden, on its northern side, is where it keeps the best of them. The Bagh-e Eram, the Garden of Paradise, was laid out in the nineteenth century by a local ruling family, the Qavams, around a handsome two-storey pavilion with painted tiles and a deep portico. A long pool in front reflects the building, and the tall cypress trees on either side give the place a feeling of balance and calm. The garden is part of the group of nine Persian gardens listed by UNESCO in 2011, and today it belongs to the university and is also a botanical garden.

The Persian garden is a place where water and shade are the point. The four-part design comes from the idea of paradise, and a stroll through the cypress, citrus and rose beds gives you a sense of why. Orange trees line the paths, and the scent of blossom in spring is overwhelming. The garden is crowded on Fridays and holidays, with families on picnics and photographers, and quieter on weekday mornings.

The city has many other things to offer. The tombs of the poets Hafez and Saadi, both much loved, draw crowds who come to recite verses and to seek a poem in a divination ritual. The old bazaar, the Vakil mosque with its tiled prayer hall and the Nasir al-Mulk mosque with its colourful glass are all worth a visit. Persepolis, the ancient Persian capital, lies about sixty kilometres to the north-east, and Sarvestan, with its Sasanian palace, a bit farther along the road.

Riding in Shiraz is not for the nervous. The traffic is dense and fast, with motorbikes, taxis and trucks weaving through the lanes, and the rules are loosely observed. Outside the city, the roads are better, and the countryside, with vineyards, orchards and mountains, is lovely. The city, with its one and a quarter million people, has plenty of fuel, and nearby Marvdasht, with a hundred and fifty thousand, is the main town on the road to Persepolis.

Spring is the best time for the gardens, with blossom and mild weather. Summer is hot, and winter can be chilly. Check current rules for foreign riders before planning a trip.
t.royal mound 10@26.2,50.5:
The mounds at Hayr Shtayyah are part of something that is hard to grasp until you see it from above: the largest ancient burial landscape in the Gulf. Across the island of Bahrain, tens of thousands of low, rounded mounds, made of stone and sand, are scattered across the desert and in places, they stretch to the horizon. They were built mostly by the Dilmun civilisation, in the third and second millennia BC, when Bahrain was a rich trading hub between Mesopotamia and the Indus valley, and UNESCO has listed a selection of these burial grounds as World Heritage.

Dilmun was famous in Mesopotamian texts as a pure, blessed land, a place of eternal life. Its wealth came from copper, pearls and the sweet water springs that rose from under the seabed and watered the date groves. The mounds hold chambers of stone slabs where the dead were laid, often with pottery, jewellery and small items of daily life. Many were looted in antiquity, but some, like the royal mounds at A'ali, are huge and imposing. Excavation has shown that families of status used the larger mounds, while ordinary people were buried in smaller ones.

The coordinates here sit between the towns of Madinat Isa and Ar Rifa'a, on the quiet southern edge of the built-up area. Roads in Bahrain are smooth and fast, with wide dual carriageways, many roundabouts and a heavy dose of speed cameras, and driving standards can be assertive. The island is small, so everything is close. Summer is very hot and humid, with temperatures above forty degrees, so go in the cooler months from November to March, early in the morning. Sandstorms can reduce visibility.

Fuel is easy to find and cheap by European standards, with stations on every main road, and workshops and cafes are plentiful. The King Fahd Causeway links Bahrain to Saudi Arabia, and the Bahrain International Circuit at Sakhir hosts Formula One. The Tree of Life, a lone mesquite tree growing in the desert, is another quirky stop. Carry water, wear a hat, and respect the sites by staying off the mounds. A glass of cardamom coffee and some dates are a fine way to finish the day.
t.dunedin@-45.9,170.5:
Dunedin is a Scottish city that happened to be built at the bottom of the world. Settlers of the Free Church of Scotland arrived in 1848 and named it after the old Gaelic name for Edinburgh, Dùn Èideann; they planted churches, a university and a great many stone buildings on the steep green hills around Otago Harbour. The gold rush of the 1860s brought money and made it for a time the richest town in the colony, which explains the Victorian railway station and the grand Octagon at the centre.

The streets are the first thing a rider notices. Dunedin climbs. Baldwin Street, in the northern suburbs, once claimed the title of the world's steepest residential street, and while that crown has since passed to a rival in Wales, it is still alarming to stand at the bottom and look up. On a motorcycle, ordinary hills give you a taste of it, with gradients that make you glad of a good clutch. Cars park on the slopes, one-way systems can confuse, and the weather is changeable: bright sun, wind and a cold shower can arrive within an hour, a local habit known as four seasons in one day.

The best ride out is along the Otago Peninsula, where a narrow road follows the harbour edge past Portobello, twelve kilometres from the city centre, and climbs onto the ridge for views of both the harbour and the open Pacific. The road has plenty of bends and few places to overtake, so go gently and enjoy the water. At the end of the peninsula, northern royal albatross nest at Taiaroa Head, a rare mainland colony, and you can see yellow-eyed penguins and fur seals on certain beaches if you keep your distance.

Dunedin is a large city with fuel on every main road, supermarkets, and a range of cafés, with student coffee bars around the university and the old brick warehouse district near the harbour. Traffic here keeps left, and speed limits are strictly applied, so relax and enjoy the Scottish gloom.

From here the Southern Scenic Route heads south through the Catlins, so top up before you go, because pumps become scarce once the coast road takes over.
t.segment jayllihuaya ichu@-15.9,-69.9:
Puno sits on the shore of Lake Titicaca at about 3,800 metres, and the stretch between Jayllihuaya and Ichu runs along the edge of town into the open altiplano. Jayllihuaya is a district on the western side of Puno; Ichu is the name of a river and of the tough bunch grass, ichu, that blankets the high plateau and feeds llamas, alpacas and the little sheep that wander the verges. The label belongs to the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road system that tied this far southern province, Collasuyu, to Cusco, and the old trail is the thread that connects these segments.

The altiplano is a strange, spare country to ride. The land is wide and almost treeless, ringed by distant ranges, with the lake lying cold and blue like a sheet of steel. The air is thin enough that a small engine loses real power and you feel the effort in your own lungs. Sunlight is fierce, nights drop below freezing for much of the year, and the weather changes in minutes: a hailstorm can sweep across the plain while the next valley stays dry. Wind is steady, and on the open straights it pushes a bike sideways.

The roads here are mostly paved but often patched, with livestock, shared taxis and heavy trucks hauling goods to and from the Bolivian border at Desaguadero. Dogs and sheep on the road are common, and villages have speed bumps that come without much warning. In the rainy season, from December to March, the plains flood in places and the nights are less cold; from May to September the skies are brilliantly clear and the mornings bitter.

Puno is a city of well over a hundred thousand, so fuel, hotels and food are easy to find, with grilled trout from the lake and quinoa soup in plain restaurants. The reed islands of the Uros people and the stone burial towers at Sillustani, built by pre-Inca Colla people on a peninsula in Lake Umayo, are within reach of a half-day ride and both are well worth the time.

Sleep a night in Puno before riding further, since the altitude can give you a pounding headache otherwise.
t.al jalahma house@26.2,50.6:
Muharraq is the old island city of Bahrain, joined to Manama by causeways, and for most of the last few thousand years it was the place where the country's real wealth came from. That wealth was pearls. The natural oyster beds of the Gulf were among the richest in the world, and in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries the merchants of Muharraq exported pearls to Bombay, Paris and beyond. The money built houses, and a handful of those houses are now part of a UNESCO-listed trail that follows the pearling economy from boat to dealer to home.

The Jalahma house belongs to that group. Houses of this type were built of coral stone and gypsum plaster, with thick walls to keep out the heat, and they were organised around inner courtyards where family life went on out of sight. Roofs were carried on mangrove poles brought from East Africa, carved teak doors came from India, and wind towers caught the breeze and sent it down into the rooms. A wealthy merchant's house was designed to impress from the street yet remain private inside, with a majlis, a reception room, where business was done over coffee and dates. Some of these houses have been restored with care and others are waiting for their turn, so you may find open doors in one lane and shuttered windows in the next.

The area around is a maze of narrow lanes in the old quarter, where cars crawl and bikes can squeeze, but heat and glare reduce the appeal of riding in the afternoon. Go in the morning, when the sun is low, or after sunset, when the lanes are lit and the cafés fill with men playing dominoes. The best season is November to March, when daytime temperatures are pleasant. Summer is brutal, with heat and humidity that can top forty degrees and make metal too hot to touch.

Fuel is cheap and easy to find, with stations on all main roads in Muharraq, and the island has plenty of small restaurants and cafés where you can try fish with spiced rice. Dress modestly, particularly around mosques and in the old market, and ask permission before photographing people. The call to prayer, rising from several mosques at once in the evening, is the proper soundtrack to the old town.
t.pearling@26.2,50.6:
Pearling is the idea behind the whole route, not a single building, and the point on this map marks the heart of the old pearl trade in Muharraq. For centuries, divers set out from here each summer on wooden boats to work the oyster beds in the shallow Gulf, and the season, the long dive, lasted from about June to September. A diver went down with a clip on his nose, a stone to take him to the bottom, and a basket for the oysters, holding his breath for a minute or more and repeating the dive dozens of times a day. A rope hauled by a companion on deck brought him back up. The work was hard, the pay was poor, and many divers were in debt to the boat captain, the nokhada, for the whole of their working lives.

Singing was part of the work. A man called the naham sang to the crew, keeping rhythm and spirit up, and those songs survive in a living folk tradition that is still performed in Bahrain. The oyster beds, called hayr, were located by long experience, and the shallow banks off the north coast of Bahrain were known as some of the best in the Gulf. The trade collapsed in the 1930s when Japanese cultured pearls flooded the market, and at the same time oil was found in Bahrain, in 1932. The country's economy changed forever, but the memory of the pearling age is a source of pride, and the UNESCO route traces it through a seafront, an oyster warehouse, merchants' houses and a fort.

The route is a walking one, and the riding is a way to get there. The roads around Muharraq are generally good, with wide new boulevards on the outskirts and narrow lanes in the old quarter. The shore road offers a view of the water that was the working world of the divers, and the best light is early morning, when the sea turns pale and the dhows rest at their moorings. The sea breeze helps a little, but from June to September the humidity is severe and midday riding is hard work.

Muharraq, with nearly a hundred thousand people, has fuel stations and cafés in abundance. Sit down for a glass of karak tea, sweet and spiced, or Arabic coffee with cardamom, and look at the water. t.fakhro house@26.2,50.6:
The Fakhro house belongs to a group of houses of the pearl merchants of Muharraq, and it is a good excuse to talk about the town in which they stand. Muharraq was Bahrain's capital until the early twentieth century, and its old quarter keeps the layout that the town had when the pearl trade ruled everything. Lanes, called sikkas, wind between high walls of coral stone and plaster, deliberately narrow and twisting so that the shade of one house falls across the next and the sea breeze is funnelled through. In a hot, damp climate, urban design meant survival.

Walking, or riding slowly, through these lanes gives you a feel for how intimate the quarter is. Doors are tall and heavy, studded with metal and carved in patterns, with a small door set into a larger one for everyday use. Decorative plasterwork and carved wood cover the upper parts of the walls, and windows are fitted with wooden shutters or latticework that lets air in while keeping eyes out. On corners stand small neighbourhood mosques, and small shops sell sweets, spices and household goods. In some lanes you will find a group of old men sitting outside a café, watching you with polite interest.

Restoration has been uneven. Some houses have been carefully repaired and opened to visitors, with painted ceilings and carefully restored rooms, while others stand empty with sagging balconies, and the contrast is part of the place's charm. UNESCO inscription in 2012 helped, and the programme is still unfinished. For the traveller, the thing to do is simply to follow the lanes, look at the doorways, and stop in the cafés. Halwa, a sticky sweet made of starch, sugar, nuts and spices, is the local speciality, and it comes in many flavours.

Riding here is gentle. Streets are narrow and shared with pedestrians, and a slow pace is not only polite but necessary. Park near the main road and walk if the lanes become too tight. Fuel stations are easy to find on the main roads around the island, and there is nothing in the old quarter itself. Pleasant weather lasts from November to March, and the middle of the day in summer is best spent indoors. In the evening, the quarter wakes up again, with lights in the windows and the smell of grilled fish drifting from the side streets.
t.al alawi house@26.2,50.6:
Muharraq's most famous export after pearls is probably football, and the Al-Alawi house stands in a quarter where every wall seems to have a team scarf hanging from it. The Muharraq club is one of the most successful in the country, with a loyal following, and on match days the cafés and lanes of the old town are noisy with argument and song.
