The house itself is another example of the architecture of the pearl-trade era, made of coral stone and plaster, with wooden balconies, carved doors and an inner courtyard. What is striking about the houses on this route is how modest the street front often is. Wealth was kept inside, and the plain facade gave nothing away. Inside, painted ceilings, carved wooden niches and tall windows made rooms that were cool even in midsummer, and an air of calm hung over the whole.

The island is also home to Bahrain's international airport, and aircraft pass low over the old town at times. The mix is odd and typical of the country: ancient mud and stone alongside modern engineering, a skyline of cranes and towers on the horizon, and fishing boats pulled up in a creek between the two. Riders will find the roads around Muharraq wide and well surfaced, with plenty of roundabouts and traffic lights, but the drivers can be fast and sudden. Take care at junctions, because lane changes happen without signals.

Cafés in the old quarter are the place to rest. Order Arabic coffee, poured in small cups from a long-spouted pot, and a plate of dates, and sit outside if the weather allows. Local fish and rice dishes, such as machboos with spiced fish or prawns, are the dishes to try, and the shops sell honeyed sweets for the road. Fuel is cheap, with stations on the main roads and the ring around the island. The cooler months, from November to March, are the time to come. Ramadan changes the rhythm of the town, with quiet days and lively nights, and shops closing and reopening on a different timetable.
t.badr ghulum house@26.2,50.6:
Badr Ghulum house is the last of the Muharraq pearl houses on this list, and it is a good place to say something about the island as a whole. Muharraq is small, flat and low, joined by causeways to Manama and, farther south, to the main island of Bahrain, and the whole country of Bahrain is a little archipelago in the Gulf,. From here a longer causeway runs west to Saudi Arabia, and it carries heavy traffic at weekends, which gives the island a feeling of being at a crossroads.

The climate is the main thing to plan around. Summer days are long, humid and extremely hot, with the sea warm as a bath and little relief at night. Winter is mild, between about fifteen and twenty-five degrees, with occasional rain, and wind from the north-west called the shamal that raises dust and cools the air. Wise riders set off at dawn or after dusk, wear light-coloured gear with ventilation and carry water at all times. Sandstorms can reduce visibility sharply, and a day with a brown haze is not a day for the causeway.

The architecture of the house follows the same pattern as the others on the trail, built around a courtyard with high walls and decorative plaster, and it has a story of its own that the on-site displays explain better than any guide. What you see more clearly from this part of town is the transition between old and new, with the glass towers of the financial district on the skyline across the water and the low houses of the old quarter close at hand. The Bahrain International Circuit, where the Formula One Grand Prix is held each spring, lies on the main island in the desert south of Manama, and on race weekend the whole country hums.

Bahrain is easy for a rider in practical terms. Fuel is cheap and plentiful, roads are generally in excellent condition, and the distances are short. Helmets are required, and speed cameras are common. Food is varied, with Indian, Arabic and Persian cooking everywhere, and a good meal costs little. Be respectful of local customs, dress modestly in the old quarter and ask before photographing people.
t.la paz@-16.5,-68.1:
La Paz sits in a canyon, and that is the first strange thing about it. The city is the seat of Bolivia's government, and it lies at around three thousand six hundred metres, with the poorer and larger city of El Alto perched on the rim above at over four thousand. From the rim you look down into a bowl of red-brown buildings spilling down the slopes, with the great snowy peak of Illimani, over six thousand four hundred metres, standing over the southern edge like a guardian. The air is thin, so arrive early, rest a day and drink coca tea, which locals swear by and which really does help a little.

The road everybody comes for begins here. The North Yungas Road, known as the Death Road, leaves La Paz, climbs to the pass of La Cumbre at around forty-six hundred metres and then drops, in a little over sixty kilometres, to the subtropical town of Coroico at about twelve hundred metres. That is a descent of well over three thousand metres, from bare grassland and cold fog into steaming cloud forest, and the road clings to cliffs that fall away for hundreds of metres. In the 1990s an international bank labelled it the most dangerous road in the world, and trucks and buses did regularly go over the edge. A modern paved road now carries most of the traffic, so the old track is quieter, and most of its visitors are cyclists and riders who come for the thrill.

Riding it needs care. The surface is gravel and rock, often wet, with water running across it from waterfalls, and the edge is unprotected in many places. Traffic keeps to the left on this stretch so that the driver on the cliff side can see the wheel, a custom that surprises visitors. Fog, rain and mud change the picture hour by hour, and late afternoon is a poor time to start. A small fee is charged at the entrance to the road, and it is wise to ride with a guide or at least with another rider.

Fuel in La Paz is easy to find, though quality varies, and it is wise to top up in the city or El Alto before leaving. Carry water, a rain layer and warm clothing for the top, because the temperature difference between the pass and the bottom is huge. The best season is the dry months, from May to October. Between December and March the rains make the road treacherous.
t.amarat yousif a fakhro@26.2,50.6:
Muharraq, the island where this house stands, is a flat knob of coral and sand just off the north coast of Bahrain, and in the age of pearls it was one of the richest places in the Gulf. The Fakhro family were among the merchants who made money in that trade, and their house, the Amarat Yousif Fakhro, is part of the Pearling Path, a group of buildings in the old town that UNESCO inscribed in 2012 as a testimony to the island economy that depended on pearls for centuries.

To understand why the house matters, think of how the business worked. Every summer, fleets of wooden boats left Muharraq for the oyster beds offshore, and the men on board dived by hand to the sea floor, held their breath for a minute or two, and came up with oysters in a basket. Merchants on land advanced money to the captains, bought the pearls, and sold them on to dealers in Bombay and beyond. The big merchant houses grew out of this credit system, and their buildings show it: tall rooms for receiving guests, strong storerooms, and a layout that mixed family life with business.

Look at the materials. These houses are built of coral stone, held together with lime and plastered in gypsum, with carved teak doors imported from India, and often topped with wind towers, open shafts that catch the breeze and funnel it downwards. Narrow lanes, shaded by the walls, wind between them in a way that keeps the interior cool without any machinery. In the heat of an August afternoon the difference is something you can feel on your skin. The houses are slowly being restored, and a few are open as museums, although times vary and are worth checking.

Riding on the island is slow, with narrow one-way lanes, parked cars and children playing football, and the best way to see the Pearling Path is to leave the bike and walk. The wider roads around Muharraq carry heavy traffic, and Bahraini drivers are quick. Fuel is cheap and easy to find in Muharraq and Manama, a few minutes away. Eat at a small cafe in the old town, order karak tea or Arabic coffee, and try a plate of machboos, the spiced rice and meat dish that is the Gulf's version of a national meal. Winter, from November to March, is the pleasant season, since summer humidity can be hard to take.
t.qal at bu mahir@26.2,50.6:
Bu Mahir is where Muharraq meets the sea, and for a pearling island that is the point. The fort stands near the southern tip of the island, on a spit of land that once looked straight out over the shallow water where the oyster beds lie, and the rest of the pearling story, the merchant houses and the shops, lies behind it in the lanes of the old town. Today reclaimed land and a modern shoreline have pushed the water back, so the view is not what it was, but the feeling of being on an edge survives.

The pearling season was brutal and short. When it began in early summer, the whole fleet put to sea from this stretch of coast, with the boats loaded with water, rice, dates and crew, and families waving from the shore. Divers stayed at sea for months. In the old accounts the departure was a great public event, with songs, drums and the captain's call. When the boats came back at the end of the season, the town celebrated and the debts were settled, for better or worse. Seen from the spit, the shallow, greenish water and the flat horizon explain a good deal of Bahrain's character.

The fort itself is a modest piece of military architecture, small and plain, built to guard the approach from the water. It sits within the Pearling Path inscription, which includes the seashore here along with the oyster beds and the merchants' buildings. Visiting is simple. A small cafe nearby is usually open in the evening, and the air is full of the smell of salt, diesel and frying fish. At dusk the sun sinks behind the Manama skyline across the bay, and the light goes copper.

On a bike, you will arrive by the coastal road through Muharraq, with slow traffic, parked cars and the occasional goat on a leash, and you should expect a hot, humid, windless day for much of the year. The shamal, the northwesterly wind, can bring dust and rough water in winter and early summer. Fuel is available on the main roads on the island and in nearby Manama. The best time is the cooler months, from November to March, in the late afternoon, when the heat has lifted and you can walk the shore in comfort.
t.nukhidhah house@26.3,50.6:
In pearling, the captain was the nukhidhah, and he was everything: navigator, banker, judge and, for months at a time, the only authority a hundred men would see. The word comes from Persian and travelled across the Gulf with the trade. A house that carries the name belonged to one of those men, or to his family, in the old town of Muharraq, and it stands as a reminder of how the pearling hierarchy worked, from the captain at the top to the divers and rope-pullers underneath.

The system was hard and elaborate. Divers, called ghaus, worked in pairs with a rope-puller, the saib, who hauled up the diver and his basket from the sea floor. A nose clip of turtle shell and a stone weight were the only equipment. Boys served as helpers, and a ship's singer, the nahham, sang to keep the crew's rhythm. The captain advanced money against the season's catch, and a poor season could leave families in debt for years. The life behind the elegant carved doors was therefore one of both profit and risk, and the best houses mirror that confidence, with courtyards for meetings and rooms for storing supplies.

When you step into the lanes of Muharraq, notice how the buildings are designed for air. Walls of coral stone are thick and pale, doors are tall, and narrow lanes funnel the breeze. Wind towers, where they survive, stand up like chimneys. The district is not a museum frozen in time: ordinary families live next door, and the rhythm of the day, school runs, shop shutters, evening football, goes on around the heritage buildings. Be quiet, be polite and keep your helmet off.

Muharraq sits right beside the airport and the causeway to Manama, so the roads are busy and the junctions confusing, with roundabouts and quick lane changes. Ride slowly in the old town and park outside the lanes. Fuel stations are plentiful nearby. Coffee houses in the district serve Arabic coffee and sweet tea, and a plate of balaleet, vermicelli sweetened with sugar and saffron and served with an omelette, makes an excellent breakfast. Go in winter, in the morning, before the heat and the tourist groups arrive.
t.qal at al bahrain ancient harbour and ca:
Qal'at al-Bahrain is a hill, and the hill is made of cities. For about four thousand years, people have built on this spot on the north coast of Bahrain, and every generation has laid its houses and walls on top of the one before, until the mound, called a tell, rose over the surrounding palm gardens. Archaeologists have peeled back the layers to find the capital of the Dilmun civilisation, a trading power of the Bronze Age that linked Mesopotamia with the Indus valley, with Bahrain as the entrepot where copper, pearls, timber and grain changed hands. UNESCO listed the site in 2005.

On top of this ancient mound stands a stone fort that most visitors photograph first. The Portuguese took control of Bahrain in 1521 and built or rebuilt a fortress here, and later rulers, Persian and Arab, held it in turn. The walls are of rough local stone, with a moat that once filled with seawater, and the towers look out over the Gulf. The little museum at the foot of the site shows the objects found in the excavations, including pottery, seals and tools, and gives a clear sense of how far back the story goes.

The setting is flat and hot, so go late in the day. The fort stands above a stretch of shore where fishing boats still launch, and from the walls you can see the skyline of Manama to the east, with the towers of the financial district rising out of the haze. At sunset the light turns the old stone the colour of honey. Palm gardens surround the base of the tell, still watered by springs, and the smell of damp earth and sea is strong when the wind comes from the north.

Riding here is easy: the coast road from Manama runs along the shore, with straight, flat stretches, roundabouts and a steady flow of cars, and the site is clearly signposted. Parking is simple. Fuel is available in Manama and the nearby suburbs of Jidd Hafs and Madinat Isa, all within a few minutes. Opening hours change, so check before you go. Winter is the season for walking the ruins, and a cold drink from the cafe nearby tastes better than anything else on a hot day.
t.murad house@26.2,50.6:
The Murad family were pearl merchants, and their house in Muharraq belongs to the generation that saw the trade at its peak and then watched it collapse. The business boomed in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, as demand for natural pearls rose in Europe and India, and the merchants of the Gulf grew rich. Then, in the 1930s, the Japanese perfected the cultured pearl, prices fell, and the industry went into a decline from which it never recovered. In Bahrain the crash was cushioned by oil, struck in 1932, the first oil strike on the Arab side of the Gulf.

The result is that the old houses of Muharraq are a record of a vanished prosperity. The family names on them, the Siyadis, the Murads, the Fakhros, belong to merchants who bankrolled voyages, built mosques and set up the town's institutions. Their houses are the best evidence, with their carved wooden doors, plaster ornament and shaded courtyards, and the care that has gone into restoring them has given the neighbourhood back some dignity. The restoration was carried out for the UNESCO listing in 2012.

You will find the lanes tight and the buildings close, and it is best explored on foot with a bottle of water. Look up for the wooden balconies and the decorative gypsum panels, and look at the detail in the door frames. The sounds are from daily life, a radio from an open window, shoes on stone, the call to prayer from one of several mosques. It is a living neighbourhood, so be discreet with a camera and avoid blocking doorways.

For a rider, Muharraq island is small and the roads are busy, with school traffic in the morning and heavy congestion in the late afternoon. Park on the wider streets and walk. Fuel is cheap and easy to find, with stations on the main roads in Muharraq and Manama. The island is also home to the airport, so you will hear aircraft overhead. Summer is hot and humid, and the best months are from November to March. In the evening, look for a cafe serving halwa, the sweet, sticky Bahraini dessert flavoured with saffron and cardamom, which is the island's most famous sweet.
t.siyadi mosque@26.3,50.6:
Muharraq has many mosques, and the Siyadi Mosque is one that people stop for even if they never go in. It was built by the Siyadi family, who were among the leading pearl merchants of the island, and it stands in the old quarter among their houses and shops, a plain white building whose simplicity is the whole point. In the Gulf, a merchant who had done well was expected to give something back, and a mosque was the obvious gift.

What you notice from outside is the proportion. The walls are smooth and pale, the doorways tall and narrow, the windows small, and the whole composition has a calm, upright look that suits the narrow lane it faces. There is little ornament, and that makes the details stand out: the wooden shutters, the carved lintels, the way the plaster catches the light. It is a working mosque, so the doors are open to worshippers, and visitors should respect prayer times and ask before going in.

Listen as well as look. In Muharraq the call to prayer comes from several mosques at once, a little out of step with each other, and in the old town it carries between the walls and echoes in the lanes. Dawn and dusk are the moments when the light and sound combine best. In the heat of the day the lanes are empty, apart from a cat or two, and the shop shutters are down.

Getting here by motorbike is simple enough, since the island is small and the causeways link it quickly to Manama. Inside the old quarter, though, the lanes are very narrow, some barely wide enough for a car, with blind corners and sudden crossings, so leave the bike on a wider street and walk the last bit. Fuel is cheap and plentiful on the main roads of Muharraq and Manama. Dress modestly, cover shoulders and knees, and move quietly near the prayer hall. In summer the humidity is heavy, and the cooler months from November to March are far better. Afterwards, find a small cafe nearby and drink the local tea, strong, sweet, and often flavoured with cardamom, and let the quiet settle.
t.core zone 1@26.2,50.5:
Core zone is bureaucratic language, and the thing it describes is simply the heart of the hill: the central area of the Qal'at al-Bahrain archaeological site, where the oldest and most important remains lie. It sits on the north coast of Bahrain, between the shore and the palm gardens, and a short distance from the suburbs of Jidd Hafs and Madinat Isa. The idea of a core zone, with a buffer around it, is how UNESCO protects its sites from being swallowed by the surrounding city, and this one was marked out when the site was inscribed in 2005.

What is under your feet matters more than what is on the surface. Excavations here have cut down through seven main layers of occupation, going back to around 2300 BC, and they show a town that grew into a city, with walls, a street plan, houses, a harbour, and a grand building that may have been an administrative centre. Dilmun was a trading society that sat between the Mesopotamian cities and the civilisation of the Indus, and the pottery, seals and weights found here prove it. The Bronze Age is not abstract here: you can see the stones that built it.

Walk slowly. The ground is dusty, uneven and exposed, and the sun reflects hard from the pale stone. Look for the exposed walls, the foundations of houses, and the places where archaeologists have left their trenches open. A hat, sunscreen and water matter far more than a good camera. In the evening, the sky turns pink and the shadows lengthen, and the details of the ruins stand out.

The approach is easy. From Manama a coastal road runs west along the shore, flat, straight, with roundabouts and moderate traffic, and the site is signposted. Fuel is available in the suburbs nearby, and there is usually a cafe or kiosk at the visitor area, though I would not rely on it. Winter is the right season. In summer the heat is merciless, and the walk to the tell becomes an endurance test. If you have a choice, come late in the afternoon, and stay for the lights at sunset, when the old fort on the summit glows and the Gulf behind it fades from blue to grey.
t.siyadi shops@26.2,50.6:
The Siyadi family did not only build mosques and houses; they also built shops, and the row of old shops in Muharraq is a reminder that a pearl merchant was also a businessman who understood the value of property. Streets of single-storey units, with wooden shutters and plain fronts, stand near the family's other buildings in the old town, and they once held traders selling cloth, rice, spices, dates and the everyday goods a town needs. Pearls themselves were usually sold privately, in the majlis, to buyers who knew what they were doing.

Walk past with an eye for the small details: the thick wooden doors, the iron hinges, the lintels cut from a single beam, the way the walls are built of coral rock and covered in plaster, a material that breathes and keeps the heat out. The shopfronts were designed to open wide in the morning and close at night, and to give the shade of a deep overhang to anyone passing underneath. Today some are restored and used as cafes or workshops, and some are quiet.

The surrounding district is one of those places where you can feel how a town grew. Streets are narrow, houses lean together, and shops face lanes that are barely wide enough for two people to pass. Mosques, schools and bakeries stand within a few steps of each other, and the shape of the neighbourhood is the shape of the old pearling community. Look at the shadow, not just the wall, because in a hot climate shade was the real architecture.

Visiting by motorbike is simple on the main roads of Muharraq island but frustrating in the lanes, which are narrow, one-way in places and filled with parked cars. Leave the bike on a wider road and walk. Fuel is easy to find in Muharraq and Manama, a short ride away, and there are small shops selling water and snacks. Mornings and evenings are the pleasant times, before the heat and after sunset, when the lanes fill with people. Winter is far kinder than summer, when humidity makes the air feel heavy. If you are hungry, find a bakery selling fresh khubz, flat bread, and a plate of local fish, and eat in the shade.
t.al ghus house@26.2,50.6:
The word ghus is connected with diving, and the house that carries it sits in the old pearling quarter of Muharraq as a quiet counterpart to the grand merchant mansions around it. Behind the display of wealth in the big houses was the work of the divers, who were the men who actually brought up the oysters, and any serious visit to the Pearling Path has to include some thought for them. The merchants made money, but the divers took the risks.

Diving was done without any equipment beyond a nose clip, a stone weight to carry the diver down, a leather glove and a basket. A diver would hold his breath for a minute or two, descend perhaps ten to twenty metres, gather as many oysters as he could, and tug the rope to be hauled up, and he would repeat this dozens of times in a day. The season lasted through the hottest months, with poor food, little rest and constant ear and eye problems, and many divers began their careers as boys. The songs of the sea, the fijiri, were the music of the boats, and Muharraq is still where the tradition is best kept: rhythmic singing with drums and clapping, often performed in the evenings.

Today the neighbourhood is calm and low-key. Walls of coral stone, wooden doors, and shaded courtyards give it the character of an older Gulf. Children play in the lanes, and the light changes by the hour. It is the kind of place that rewards a slow walk with no particular goal, and that is how the heritage trail was designed to be enjoyed.

Riders will find the island easy to reach, since Muharraq is linked to Manama by short causeways, but the streets in the old quarter are narrow and tricky, and parking on the wider avenues is better. Fuel is cheap and easy to find, with stations on every main road. Visit in the cooler months, from November to March, and go in the early morning or at sunset. If you hear drumming from a courtyard, stop and listen, because it may be fijiri, and you will not forget the sound. Finish with a glass of cardamom tea from a corner cafe.
t.siyadi majlis@26.3,50.6:
A majlis is a sitting room, and in the Gulf it is much more than that. It is where the men of a household received guests, drank coffee, settled disputes and did business, and in a pearl merchant's house it was the room where deals were struck. The Siyadi Majlis was part of the family's holdings in the old town of Muharraq, and it is the sort of space where you realise that pearls were sold by trust and conversation as much as by weighing and counting.

Picture the scene. Guests sat on cushions along the walls, with a brass pot of coffee, a dallah, being poured into tiny handleless cups, always a small amount, and the host would keep refilling until the guest shook the cup to signal enough. Dates and sweets were passed round. Buyers from Bombay or the other Gulf ports might arrive with a purse and a trained eye, and the sale of a fine pearl could take hours, with tea and talk until a price was settled. A good merchant's reputation depended on his hospitality and his honesty.

The room itself shows how Gulf architecture manages without machines. Thick walls keep out the sun, high ceilings let heat rise, and openings are placed to catch the breeze. Carved plaster panels, called niches, frame the walls, and a few windows with wooden shutters are arranged so air can pass but direct sunlight cannot. The care taken over details such as the frames, the doors and the ceiling beams says something about the importance of the room.

Visiting is straightforward on foot, but the old quarter is awkward for bikes, with narrow lanes, parked cars and blind corners, so park on a wider road. Fuel is cheap and easy to find across Muharraq and Manama. Opening times for restored buildings vary, so check ahead rather than assuming. The cooler season, from November to March, is the best time, and late afternoon the best hour. If somebody offers you coffee, accept, take it with your right hand, and shake the cup when you have had enough.
t.murad majlis@26.2,50.6:
Climate is the strongest force in Bahrain, and the Murad Majlis, a guest room in the old merchant quarter of Muharraq, is a good place to think about it. The island lies in the shallow western Gulf, where the sea is warm as a bath, the air is thick with moisture and summer temperatures routinely pass forty degrees. Before air conditioning, the buildings of Muharraq were the response: thick walls, shaded courtyards, tall rooms, and lanes narrow enough that the sun rarely touched the ground.

The word that Bahrainis use for the northwesterly wind is the shamal, and it blows on and off through much of the year, bringing dust and rough water in winter and early summer. In late summer the humidity becomes the main problem, with night temperatures that barely fall and a sticky stillness that wraps the whole island. A rider who has come from Europe in July will find the heat is like a hair dryer in the face, and the sensible response is the one the locals use: ride early, sit out the middle of the day, and come out again after dusk.

Winter is a different country. From November to March the days are mild, with clear skies, light winds and temperatures in the low to mid twenties, and the old town is at its best. The Murad Majlis, like its neighbours, repays a visit in the cooler months, when the doors are open, the courtyards are pleasant and there are people in the lanes. Look at the thick plastered walls, the high ceilings and the shuttered windows, and you can see how the climate drove the design.

Practical details are easy. Muharraq is small, flat and densely built, with a ring of busy roads around the old quarter. The lanes inside are narrow, with blind corners, and parking is tight, so leave the bike on a main road and go on foot. Fuel is cheap and stations are common in Muharraq and nearby Manama. Drink plenty of water, wear light clothes that cover your arms, and remember that the sun is stronger than it feels, especially with the reflection off pale walls. A cold lime and mint juice from a corner cafe is the local answer to the afternoon heat, and a good excuse to sit in the shade for a while.
t.segment socoroma sur@-18.3,-69.6:
Socoroma is a village high above the desert, and the road to it is a climb from the coast into another world. Starting from the sea at Arica, the road rises through the arid foothills, past cactus and rocky ridges, and up into the Andean altiplano, passing from sea level to the better part of three thousand metres in a couple of hours. The change is obvious: the air thins, the temperature drops, the light becomes harder and the sky turns a deeper blue. Socoroma sits on the old route between the coast and the high plateau, on terraced slopes cultivated for centuries.

The village is a working Aymara community, with a small church, stone houses with straw roofs and terraces where oregano, potatoes and maize grow. The terraces are far older than the Spanish, and the llamas that drift across the path are not for show. It is a place where local life continues at its own pace, and visitors are expected to be quiet and respectful. Mules and llamas once carried silver and goods along the trails here, and the stone-paved tracks survive in places.

The riding is where the segment earns its name. A road of long gradients, hairpins and fast sweepers climbs steadily, with the surface mostly good but often broken at the edges, and with trucks heading to the mines and the Bolivian border. Weather is changeable: clear mornings, afternoon cloud, and a chill at dusk, and in the rainy season, from December to March, thunderstorms and flash floods can close roads. Altitude is a real concern; a ride that starts at the sea and ends at 3,000 metres can cause headaches and breathlessness, so take it slowly and drink water.

Plan your fuel carefully. Arica is the last reliable place on the coast, and while there is fuel at Putre and along the main road, small villages like Socoroma have no stations. Cold nights are normal at this height, so carry warm clothing even in summer. In the village, there may be a small shop with water and snacks, but do not rely on it. The best seasons are the dry months from April to November, and the best hours are the morning and early afternoon, before the cloud builds and the wind rises.
t.sarvestan sarvestan monument@29.2,53.2:
Sarvestan lies on the dry plateau of Fars province, in the south of Iran, about ninety kilometres south-east of Shiraz, and its name means the place of cypresses. The monument that bears the name is a ruined palace or fire temple of the Sasanian period, built in the fifth century, with a great central dome and arched halls of mud brick and stone. It is often said to be one of the oldest domed buildings in the world, and its form is believed to have influenced later Islamic architecture.

The site stands in open country, beside the road, with a wide view over fields and low brown hills. The brickwork has weathered into soft, pale shapes, and the vaults still carry an air of dignity. Nearby are the remains of a small village and a few trees, and farmers work in the surrounding fields. A custodian often keeps the site, and a small fee may be asked.

The ride from Shiraz follows a long road across a high plain, with mountains in the distance and salt flats that sparkle in the sun. Lake Maharloo, east of Shiraz, turns pink in summer from salt-loving algae, a strange and beautiful sight. Fuel is available in the towns along the main road, and it is cheap by international standards, but stations can be far apart, so keep the tank full. Bring water and sun protection, because there is little shade.

The best time to ride is spring or autumn, when the temperatures are mild. Summers are fierce, and winter nights can be cold at this altitude. In Shiraz, the Bagh-e Eram, a garden of cypresses and a nineteenth-century pavilion, makes a fine contrast to this austere ruin: one all shade and water, the other all sun and stone. Together, they tell the story of Persian architecture.
t.firuzabad ardashir investiture relief@28:
The relief at Firuzabad is a stone picture of power being handed over. Carved in the early third century into a cliff face near the town, it shows Ardashir I, the founder of the Sasanian dynasty, on horseback, receiving a ring of kingship from the god Ahura Mazda, who is also mounted. Beneath the hooves of the horses lie the bodies of Ardashir's defeated enemies, the last Parthian king and, according to some readings, an evil spirit. It is a statement in rock of the new dynasty's claim to rule by divine favour.

The relief stands at the mouth of a gorge called Tang-e Ab, where a stream runs through a narrow valley of limestone cliffs and the air is cool and fresh. Firuzabad itself, a town of about 66,000 people nine kilometres away, is the place for fuel, supplies and a meal. Ardashir founded the original city of Gor here, a perfectly round city of walls and moats, whose outline can still be traced from above, and his palace, a vast domed ruin, stands to the north, with a fortress called Qal'eh Dokhtar, the Maiden's Castle, on a ridge above.

Firuzabad is also famous for its roses. The damask rose of this region is distilled into rosewater, and in spring the fields bloom pink and the air smells sweet. The road through the mountains to Firuzabad is a pleasure, with winding bends, steep cliffs and views over valleys. Surfaces are generally good, but rockfalls can occur after rain, and goats and sheep share the road.

The best time is spring, when the roses are in flower and the hills are green. Summers are hot and dry, and winter brings snow on the heights. Bring water and a hat, and give yourself time to walk through the gorge and look at the carving in the late afternoon light, when the stone warms to a golden shade.
t.bar harbor@44.4,-68.2:
Bar Harbor is the door to Mount Desert Island, the large granite island off the coast of Maine where Acadia National Park spreads over mountains, ponds and rocky shore. The town sits on Frenchman Bay, with the humped shapes of the Porcupine Islands offshore, and it has been a summer destination since the 1800s, when wealthy families from Boston and Philadelphia built huge shingle mansions they called cottages. A great fire in 1947 burned a lot of them, but the town rebuilt, and its streets are now a mix of old inns, gift shops, and lobster restaurants.

The riding starts right away. The Park Loop Road, about twenty-seven miles of one-way and two-way roads, tours the shore at Sand Beach and Thunder Hole, climbs along Jordan Pond, and branches to the summit of Cadillac Mountain, which at 1,530 feet is the highest point on the US Atlantic coast. In autumn and winter it is among the first places in the country to see the sunrise. A park pass is required for vehicles, and the loop gets crowded in July and August, so the best hours are early morning or after supper. The road surface is generally good, the speed limits low, and wildlife crossings are possible. In foggy weather, which is common, the view vanishes but the smell of spruce and sea stays.

John D. Rockefeller Jr. funded the carriage roads, a network of broken-stone paths with handsome stone bridges, and they are closed to motor vehicles, so bikes belong on the park loop instead. The granite is pink and pale, scraped by glaciers, and the rock faces plunge straight into the Atlantic.

Bar Harbor has about two and a half thousand year-round residents, and it fills with visitors and cruise-ship crowds in season, so parking is tight. Fuel is available in town, though prices are higher, and Ellsworth, about twenty-four kilometres to the north, is the nearest bigger town with larger shops and services. A lobster roll at a harbourside shack is a fair prize at the end of the day, and nights are cool even in August.
t.royal mound 8@26.2,50.5:
Mid-morning on the Bahraini plateau is quiet in a way that surprises people. The towns have emptied into offices, the wind has not yet picked up, and the only sound across the pale limestone is a distant radio from somebody's pickup. That is the best hour to come to the royal mounds at A'ali, because the gravel is still cool enough to walk on and the shapes have long shadows to define them.

Royal Mound 8 is one of a cluster of big burial mounds built by the Dilmun civilisation around four thousand years ago. What looks from the road like a rounded hill of rubble was once a carefully engineered tomb: a stone chamber, sometimes two stacked above each other, roofed with massive slabs and then buried under an earthen and stone dome. The largest of the royal mounds rise several storeys, which in a country this flat is a statement you can read from kilometres away. Who lay inside is a question archaeologists answer only in general terms, but the scale suggests people of rank, perhaps rulers, and the labour needed shows a society with surplus and power.

For a rider, the setting is simple. The tracks and sandy access roads near the mounds are short and mostly flat, but sand blown across tarmac is the real hazard, because it behaves like fine gravel under a front tyre. Approach junctions slowly and keep your line straight. Heat is the other issue: from May to September midday temperatures can pass forty degrees with humidity to match, so ride early or late, carry water, and remember that black leather and a helmet turn a parked bike into an oven.

Everything practical is close. Madinat Isa, about three kilometres away, is a planned town of apartment blocks and shopping streets with petrol stations, cafés and supermarkets, and fuel in Bahrain is plentiful and cheap by European standards. Do not expect shade at the site itself.

Before you leave, take a minute to climb a low rise nearby and look across the fields. Rows of smaller mounds run out into the haze like waves, and it takes a moment to realise that you are standing in a graveyard that once held many thousands of burials.
t.manama@26.2,50.6:
An afternoon in Manama begins with a lesson in geography that the map sometimes hides: the Al Zubarah of the ride's name is not in Bahrain. It is a ruined pearling and trading town on the north-west coast of Qatar, a short sea crossing away but with no road between the two countries, so no rider will get there from here. What links them is a family. In 1783 the Al Khalifa, who had built up Zubarah, moved across the water and took Bahrain, and their descendants still rule. So the afternoon in Manama is best spent seeing where that move led.

The capital is compact and busy, a mixture of old and new that rewards a slow wander. The old centre is organised around Bab al-Bahrain, the Gate of Bahrain, a colonial-era arch built in the 1940s at what was then the water's edge, and behind it the souq runs through a maze of lanes selling spices, gold, perfume, textiles and tea. Beyond, the skyline is a mixture of glass towers, including the World Trade Center with its three wind turbines slung between the towers, and the huge white dome of the Al Fateh Grand Mosque, one of the largest in the region and open to visitors outside prayer times. The National Museum on the waterfront tells the island's story from the Dilmun period to the present.

Riding in Manama requires patience. The streets of the old centre are narrow and one-way, the main roads are fast and crowded, and the flyovers can be confusing, so give yourself time and use a navigation app. Parking for motorcycles is usually informal, so choose a spot out of the way of traffic and well away from pedestrians. Summer afternoons are fierce, and shade is rare, so keep water close. Cameras watch most of the major roads.

Fuel is easy, with stations throughout the city, and the food is excellent. Look for machboos, a spiced rice dish with chicken or fish, and fresh dates and halwa, a gelatinous sweet in a rainbow of colours. In the evening the restaurants of Adliya, a district of galleries and cafés, are lively and varied.

The Corniche at dusk, with the lights of the towers reflected in the bay, makes a pleasant end to the day.
t.a ali east burial mound field@26.1,50.5:
Walk away from the big royal mounds and the landscape changes character completely. The east field at A'ali is not about individual monuments but about quantity: a vast scatter of small and medium mounds, hundreds of them, spreading across the gravel plain like the humps of a school of whales. Some are intact, others have slumped or been opened, and many have been nibbled at by roads, houses and farms. The effect is of a landscape in which the dead outnumbered the living by a huge margin.

At its height, Bahrain is thought to have had several hundred thousand burial mounds, one of the densest concentrations of prehistoric graves in the world. Over the last century, development has destroyed most of them, and what survives is a fraction of the original total, which makes the fields at A'ali especially precious. The area was included in the UNESCO World Heritage listing in 2019 as part of a series of Dilmun burial sites, and fences and signs now mark the protected zones.

The scale of this burial landscape raises questions that archaeologists are still working to answer. Why were so many people buried on an island that was probably home to only a few thousand? One theory is that the island was seen as sacred and that the dead of neighbouring regions were brought here, an idea supported by the mythology of Dilmun as a holy land. Another is that the mounds accumulated over many centuries, and the population was larger than assumed. No one knows for certain.

The ride is quick and flat from Madinat Hamad or Madinat Isa, along wide roads with plenty of roundabouts. Dust and sand blow across the tarmac, so watch your front tyre on corners, and keep an eye on traffic emerging from side roads. In the cooler months the gravel plain is a pleasant place to pause, with a view of the mounds under a pale sky.

Madinat Hamad, about four kilometres away, has the fuel, food and cash machines you will need. Come at sunrise, with a thermos if you have one, and the field is at its most evocative.
t.royal mound 2@26.2,50.5:
The man who put these mounds on the international map was a Dane with a shovel. In 1953 an expedition from Aarhus, led by Peter Glob and the young archaeologist Geoffrey Bibby, came to Bahrain to see whether the island's countless burial mounds hid anything of interest. Bibby later wrote a lively book about the work, Looking for Dilmun, and it is still the best introduction to the place, a story of heat, flies, tea and slowly dawning realisation that this dry island had been the centre of a lost trading civilisation.

Royal Mound 2 sits in the cluster at A'ali, a few kilometres from Madinat Isa. Like its neighbours, it was built from local limestone slabs and rubble, then covered with earth, and its burial chamber was entered from the side by a passage that was sealed after the funeral. By the time the Danish team arrived, almost all of the royal tombs had been looted in antiquity, so the finds were thin: scraps of pottery, fragments of ivory and the odd copper object. What mattered was the pattern. Taken together, the mounds, the walled town at Qal'at al-Bahrain and the temples at Barbar told a story of a major entrepôt linking Mesopotamia with the Indus valley.

The ground you ride over to reach the mound is part of the same story. Bahrain is a low island of pale limestone with a thin cover of sand, and everything is visible: tyre tracks, camel prints, the shadows of old walls. Roads around the mounds are mostly paved with occasional drifts of sand, and the speed limits on the local streets are low and enforced with cameras. Madinat Isa has the services you need, including fuel, food and a quick coffee.

Come in winter if you can, between November and March, when daytime temperatures sit in the low twenties and the desert smells of dust and a faint salt tang from the sea. Be respectful on site; it is a UNESCO World Heritage monument, so keep to the paths and take nothing but photographs.
t.royal mound 5@26.2,50.5:
Mound 5 has a neighbour that is much newer and much larger: Madinat Isa, or Isa Town, one of the first planned towns in the Gulf. It was laid out in the 1960s under the ruler Sheikh Isa bin Salman, a grid of wide streets, low houses and civic buildings that was meant to give a growing population modern housing. Today it feels lived in and slightly faded, with a busy market, small mosques on every corner and a long main street filled with the sound of scooters.

The mound itself stands a few minutes from this town, in a stretch of open gravel where the planners' grid gave way to the royal cemetery. It is one of a group that belong to the early Dilmun period, built roughly four thousand years ago from limestone blocks cut on the island. Bahrain has only a few small areas of high ground, and the builders took advantage of a low rise to give the mounds a commanding position. Standing beside one, you realise how much effort went into raising a tomb that most people would never enter.

Riding here is easy and unhurried. The roads are flat, wide and well signed, with roundabouts every few hundred metres, and traffic is lively but not aggressive. Be careful at junctions where drivers may cut across with little warning, and watch for sand on the tarmac after windy days. The shamal, the north-westerly wind that blows in early summer, can bring dust that reduces visibility and stings the eyes, so keep a visor handy.

Madinat Isa has about thirty-eight thousand people, and it has everything you are likely to want. Petrol stations are never far, and the small restaurants around the market serve good shawarma, grilled fish, and a strong cardamom coffee in tiny cups. The old market, the souq, has stalls that sell spices, fabrics and gold, and a walk through it makes a worthwhile contrast with the silence of the burial ground.

If you have time, visit in the late afternoon, when the light softens and the heat drains from the stone.
t.royal mound 4@26.2,50.5:
Four thousand years ago, ships sailed into the harbour at the north end of this island carrying copper from Oman, carnelian beads from the Indus valley, and grain, cloth and silver from the cities of Mesopotamia. Bahrain, which the Sumerians called Dilmun, was the middle of the trade. The mounds around A'ali, including Royal Mound 4, are the cemetery of a society that grew rich on being in the right place.

Sumerian clay tablets give Dilmun a curious reputation. In the poem of Gilgamesh, the survivor of the flood is granted immortality and sent to live at Dilmun, a place of purity and sweet water, and another myth calls it a land without sickness or death. It is a pleasant irony that one of the most celebrated paradises of ancient literature is now a dusty island of petrol stations and shopping malls, though the freshwater springs that made it so valuable do exist, rising from the seabed and from wells in the north.

The mound is a short ride from Madinat Isa along flat, well-paved roads, and the surroundings are a typical mix of limestone gravel, scrub and low houses. Navigating is simple, but the roundabouts can catch you out: local drivers use them with great confidence and not always with indicators. Slow down, make eye contact and keep a margin. If you are riding in summer, drink water before you feel thirsty, because humidity can disguise dehydration.

Visitors who want to understand the larger picture should plan a visit to Qal'at al-Bahrain, the old fort on the north coast, built on the remains of an ancient harbour town and also a World Heritage Site. From there, the Dilmun capital controlled the sea lanes and likely sent men to be buried in the mounds you see here. The distance between the two sites is not great, and the road between them passes through suburbs and palm gardens, a gentle reminder of how green this island once was.

The services in Madinat Isa are plentiful, and fuel is cheap, so there is no need to worry about range.
t.royal mound 1@26.2,50.5:
Light is the thing here, so plan around it. In the middle of the day the plateau at A'ali is a flat white glare, the mounds melt into the gravel and the heat presses down. At sunrise and the last hour before sunset, though, the low sun rakes across the surface, throwing every ridge and hollow into relief, and Royal Mound 1 turns a warm honey colour against a pale sky. Photographers know this, and you may find one or two waiting.

The mound is the first of the numbered royal tombs, part of a group of seventeen or so large mounds at the northern end of the A'ali cemetery. It is built of limestone slabs and rubble, and its dome has weathered over four thousand years into a rounded hill. At the base, you can still see the remains of the retaining wall that held the structure together. A modern fence and a low path mark the edge of the protected area, and on a quiet day the only sound is the wind.

Riding here is straightforward. The roads in and out are paved and flat, with the occasional sandy shoulder where cars have pulled off, and the nearby housing estates of Madinat Isa mean there are few long empty stretches. In the early morning the air can feel cool and damp near the coast, and a thin haze often hangs over the plateau until the sun burns it away. In winter, when the temperature falls to the low teens at night, a jacket liner is welcome.

For fuel, food and anything else, Madinat Isa is minutes away, and Bahrain's compact size means nowhere on the island is more than half an hour from a petrol station. The king's palace and the Riffa district lie to the south, and the old pearling town of Muharraq, with its traditional merchant houses, is a short ride north.

If you are planning a day on the island, I would put the mounds at the beginning, while the air is still cool and the light is kind.
t.dilmun burial mounds@26.1,50.5:
In the earliest written records of the Gulf, a land called Dilmun appears again and again. Sumerian tablets from the third millennium BC mention it as a trading partner, a source of copper and a place where certain gods were said to live. Scholars long argued over where it was, until excavations in Bahrain in the 1950s turned up a walled port city, temples and tens of thousands of graves. The match was convincing enough that Dilmun is now generally identified with Bahrain and the nearby coast of eastern Arabia.

The burial mounds are the most visible part of that civilisation. They were built between about 2200 and 1750 BC, and they range from small stone-ringed graves to the great royal mounds with their two-storey chambers. The bodies were buried in a crouched position with pottery, beads and sometimes weapons, and there is evidence of offerings made at the tombs for generations. The sheer number suggests that Bahrain was a place of special significance, and a visit makes you think about the connection between island, sea and afterlife in the minds of the people who lived here.

A short ride from the mounds takes you to Qal'at al-Bahrain, the fort and archaeological site on the north coast, which holds layers of occupation from the Dilmun period to the Portuguese in the sixteenth century. It was listed as a World Heritage Site in 2005, and it is a better place than most to understand how the old harbour town worked. The Barbar temple, west of Manama, is another Dilmun site, with an elliptical platform and a sacred spring.

Practically, Bahrain is easy and compact. Roads are good, fuel is cheap and signs are in English as well as Arabic, so you can cover the island in a day. Madinat Hamad, four kilometres from this site, is the nearest town of size.

Plan visits for the cooler months, and keep your timing flexible. In summer, the mounds are best seen first thing in the morning, before the heat sets in.
t.madinat hamad 1 burial mound field@26.1,:
Madinat Hamad is a young town built on very old ground. It was developed in the 1980s as a planned settlement, a grid of housing blocks, mosques, schools and shopping areas laid out on the desert west of A'ali, and its growth has pushed the suburbs right up to the edge of a burial field that is thousands of years old. The contrast is vivid: on one side, apartment blocks and satellite dishes; on the other, a field of rubble domes and silence.

The Madinat Hamad 1 field is one of the smaller sites in the World Heritage listing, but it is a good place to see how the mounds were distributed. They form loose clusters, with larger mounds in the centre and smaller ones around them, a pattern that suggests family or community groupings. Many have been disturbed by looters, farmers and builders, and the depressions where chambers have collapsed are visible as dark pits in the sandy surface. Unlike the royal mounds, these are the graves of ordinary people, and there is something touching in that.

For a rider, Madinat Hamad is a place of long straight roads, big roundabouts and consistent traffic. Streets are numbered in a grid, which makes navigation easy, but the sameness can be confusing, so keep your phone map handy. The main roads out of town lead to the highway to Manama and Riffa, and the interchanges are fast and busy. In the evening, the town's cafés and bakeries come alive, and the smell of grilled meat drifts from the roadside stalls.

With more than fifty thousand people, Madinat Hamad has all the services of a small city: petrol stations, supermarkets, banks and plenty of places to eat. Arabic coffee, dates and a plate of grilled fish or chicken are available at modest prices, and the portions are generous.

At the edge of the field, stand for a minute and watch the sun go down over the desert. In winter, when the air is clear, the sky can turn spectacular shades of orange and violet, and the mounds stand out as dark silhouettes against the glow.
t.royal mound 16@26.2,50.5:
Nobody knows who was buried in Royal Mound 16, and that is one of the nicest things about it. The big tombs at A'ali have been called royal for decades, because of their size and their position on the highest ground, but there is no inscription, no king's name, nothing that settles the matter. The tombs were looted long ago, probably within a few centuries of their construction, and what the robbers did not carry off was scattered by time. What remains is architecture: a vast stack of limestone, a chamber, a ramp and a silence.

Part of the pleasure of visiting lies in guessing. You can walk around the base and imagine the labour: the quarrying, the hauling, the setting of slabs weighing several tonnes each, with no iron tools and no wheeled carts that we know of. Then you notice the mound's neighbours, all within a short walk, and begin to see a landscape designed to impress. People coming up the island from the old harbour towns would have seen the tombs on the skyline and understood who ruled here.

For the rider, the site is a calm place. Roads around A'ali are straight and flat, with some low speed bumps and plenty of roundabouts, and the approach from Madinat Isa takes only a few minutes. The surface is generally good, but the gravel verge is soft and the sand on the tarmac can surprise you on corners. There is little shade and no water at the site itself, so bring a bottle. If the sun is high, wear a light scarf or cooling neck tube under your helmet.

Bahrain's population is dense, and this part of the island is surrounded by housing, so help is never far away. Madinat Isa has petrol stations, supermarkets and small restaurants, and its market is lively in the evening.

When you leave, ride slowly along the edge of the cemetery and look at the field. Hundreds of smaller mounds sit in the gravel, many opened and collapsed, each a ruined doorway to a life no one has recorded.
t.royal mound 3@26.2,50.5:
The first thing to understand about Royal Mound 3 is that it is made of the island itself. Bahrain sits on a dome of limestone, laid down in ancient seas and cracked by millions of years of sun and salt, and the builders of the mounds quarried that very stone from nearby. The slabs are pale, flaky and layered, and where a mound has collapsed you can see them stacked like old books. Up close, you may also see small fossils in the rock, shells and tiny sea creatures that lived here when the whole area lay underwater.

That geology explains much of the island's character. Limestone holds water, and beneath the surface a layer of fresh water from aquifers fed by rain in the Arabian peninsula rose in springs on the island and at sea, one reason why people settled here at all. The same stone provided building material for walls and houses, for the fort at Qal'at al-Bahrain and for the royal tombs. The core of the mound is a chamber of fitted blocks, topped with layers of rubble and sand, a design that has withstood four thousand years of weather.

Riding in this part of Bahrain is simple, but notice the surface. Where the tarmac ends, the track is hard limestone with a layer of loose fines, quite slippery on a bike with road tyres, and the verges are patched with sand. Take the dirt slowly, and use the paved approach roads wherever possible. If you pause in the middle of the day, the heat reflected off the pale ground is intense, so stop in the shade of a wall and drink.

Madinat Isa is only a few minutes away, and a fuel stop there takes no time. Bahrain's roads are well maintained, and signs are in Arabic and English, so navigation is easy, even without a phone signal.

If you have time, find a quiet corner of the site and put a hand on the stone. It has been sitting in the sun for four thousand years, and still holds the warmth of the day long after sunset.
t.royal mound 17@26.2,50.5:
Mound 17 sits on the east side of the A'ali cluster, and from here the ground slopes gently toward Ar-Rifa'a, the second great town of central Bahrain. The two places have little in common, but the combination is a good lesson in how this island has been used. One is a field of bronze age graves; the other is the seat of the ruling Al Khalifa family, who arrived from the Gulf mainland in the late eighteenth century and made Bahrain their own.

Ar-Rifa'a is divided into two parts: the old town, with its fort on a ridge above a valley and narrow lanes of traditional houses, and a newer, more modern area with large villas and golf courses. The fort, a sturdy sand-coloured building with corner towers, was a family stronghold, and visitors can usually go in when it is open. The town has cafés and restaurants, a good deal of traffic at weekends, and the kind of slightly wealthy calm that comes from tall hedges and big gates.

The riding here is gentle but busy. Roads between A'ali and Ar-Rifa'a are wide and well-surfaced, and local drivers move fast and without much fuss, so keep your speed predictable and stay out of blind spots. Watch the roundabouts and the exits to the various residential compounds, where cars can emerge suddenly. Dust is part of life here, and a pair of clear glasses or a tinted visor is useful.

Fuel is not an issue; both Ar-Rifa'a and Madinat Isa have plenty of stations, and the main roads are lined with convenience stores and bakeries. A cup of karak, strong, sweet, milky tea with cardamom, is the usual refreshment, and you will find it at almost every petrol station.

Back at the mound, take a moment to look at the way the cemetery lies on the ridge. Its position was no accident. The builders wanted their dead to look over the land and be seen from the road, and four thousand years later they are still doing exactly that.
t.royal mound 7@26.2,50.5:
Look closely at the ground around Royal Mound 7 and you will find more life than you expect. The limestone plateau looks barren from the road, but a morning visit reveals tiny desert plants gripping the cracks, lizards flicking between stones and larks running ahead of your tyres. After rare winter rain the whole area turns briefly green, with annuals and small wildflowers pushing through the gravel, and then fades again within weeks.

Bahrain's wild country is limited. Much of the island has been built over or reclaimed from the sea, but patches of desert scrub survive, with thorny acacia, ghaf trees and the toughest shrubs. The island's most famous tree, the Tree of Life, is a lone mesquite growing in the southern desert, said to be around four centuries old and still alive despite having no obvious water source. A visit takes you through a good chunk of Bahrain's dry interior and past the old oilfield that started the modern economy. Further south, Al Areen Wildlife Park protects a population of Arabian oryx and sand gazelles, and offers a glimpse of what native fauna looked like before roads and oil.

Mound 7 itself belongs to the royal cluster at A'ali, a few minutes from Madinat Isa, and is part of the UNESCO listing. For riders, the main concern in this area is surface and weather. Roads are good, but sand drifts across them in places, especially near the edges of housing developments, and there is hardly any shade. Heat, from early May until October, is tough, and the humidity along the coast can make even a short ride draining.

Fuel and food are close by. Madinat Isa has a wide choice of restaurants, from Indian and Pakistani to Lebanese and Bahraini, and a plate of machboos, the island's spiced rice and meat dish, is a good end to a day in the sun. Prices are modest, and portions are generous.

Wait for a still moment, and listen. In the quiet of early morning you can hear birds, and for a few minutes the traffic disappears.
t.a ali west burial mound field@26.1,50.5:
The west field at A'ali tells a more awkward story than its neighbour to the east, because here you can see exactly where the island's past and present collide. The mounds sit in clusters between roads and housing developments, and in places a modern wall or a road cuts straight through what was once a continuous cemetery. A mound has an electricity pylon beside it, another a rubbish bin. Bahrain is a small, crowded country with a fast-growing population, and its heritage is under constant pressure.

That pressure explains why the burial mounds were nominated for UNESCO protection. Though the island is small, it holds some of the most remarkable archaeological remains in the Gulf, and conservationists have long argued that development should be balanced against preservation. The listing in 2019 gave the sites legal and financial protection, and fences, paths and information boards now surround the main fields.

For a rider, the roads here are a pleasant mix of the modern and the mundane. Wide dual carriageways lead out to the new towns, with signs in Arabic and English and a steady stream of traffic. The tarmac is generally good, but it can be coated with sand, particularly near building sites, and drainage is poor, so after a rare rain shower puddles form quickly and the surface turns greasy. If the weather turns, take it slowly.

Madinat Hamad, about three kilometres from here, is a planned town built in the late twentieth century to house a growing population, and it has all the services you might want, including fuel, restaurants and a big shopping area. The main road between A'ali and the town is busy, but the fast lanes allow easy overtaking.

Wait until the end of the afternoon for the best light, when the sun slants low across the field and each mound casts a long shadow. If you are lucky, a dust haze catches the light and the whole scene takes on an almost painterly glow.
t.pair of royal mound 13 and 14@26.2,50.5:
Two mounds standing side by side look like a conversation, and the pair of Royal Mounds 13 and 14 has the look of one that has gone on for a long time. They sit close together in the A'ali cluster, their domes overlapping slightly at the base, and from a distance they resemble the humps of a sleeping animal. Archaeologists have noted that some of the royal tombs seem to come in groups, perhaps reflecting family relationships or generations of a ruling line, though none of this can be proved.

The mounds belong to the early Dilmun period, built around 2000 BC, when the island was a trading hub and a cultural centre. Dilmun merchants dealt in copper, pearls, dates and textiles, and the wealth that flowed through the island paid for monuments on a scale that still impresses. Pearl diving, which gave Bahrain its fame in later centuries, may have roots in the same era, and the old pearling path in Muharraq is another UNESCO site that explains how the industry shaped the island's merchant families.

Riding to the site is easy. From Madinat Isa, a short run along wide, flat roads brings you to a small car park near the fence, and you can leave the bike and walk. The ground is hard limestone with patches of loose sand, and if you step off the path in a pair of thin-soled boots you will feel it. Wind can be a problem: gusts across the plateau can be strong enough to move a bike on its side stand, so choose a sheltered spot and keep the stand on firm ground.

Services are nearby, with petrol stations in Madinat Isa and shopping malls a little further. In Bahrain, even a minor roadside stall will sell cold water, and cafés usually give a glass of water with every order, so do not hesitate to ask.

For a sense of the scale, walk around the pair slowly, counting your steps. It takes longer than you would think.
t.royal mound 9@26.2,50.5:
If you have the choice, do not come here in July. Royal Mound 9 is a good place to learn about Bahrain's summers, which are the island's real boundary condition. From June to September the air temperature rises above forty degrees, the humidity off the Gulf can reach ninety per cent, and the sun on the limestone feels like a physical weight. Local people plan their days around it, working early, sleeping through midday and emerging after sunset.

A rider has to do the same. Start before dawn, finish by ten, and avoid being on the road when the heat peaks in mid-afternoon. Carry more water than you think you need and drink it steadily, ideally with electrolytes, because sweat evaporates so quickly in the dry wind that you may not notice how much you are losing. A light, ventilated jacket is better than none, and a cooling vest worn under it makes a real difference. Tyres run hot on tarmac that can reach seventy degrees, so check pressures often.

The shamal is the other factor, a steady north-westerly that blows for days at a time in early summer and carries dust that turns the sky yellow. It reduces visibility, scours paintwork and piles sand at the edge of roads. In winter the wind turns cooler and occasionally brings rain, which makes the limestone slick, so be careful on the tarmac when the first drops fall.

The mound itself is an impressive piece of early engineering, one of more than a dozen royal tombs in the A'ali cluster, built from local limestone about four thousand years ago and designed to last. It is part of the UNESCO site, and well worth the visit in the cooler months.

Fuel and food are in Madinat Isa, a few minutes away, along with air-conditioned shopping malls that make a good place to sit out the midday heat. If you are riding in summer, treat them as part of the route.
t.royal mound 15@26.2,50.5:
Bahrain has an oil story that is gentler than most. Oil was found in 1932, at Jebel Dukhan in the south of the island, the first strike on the Arabian side of the Gulf, and the royalties began a transformation that has since filled the plateau with roads, flats and refineries. Compared with its neighbours, Bahrain's reserves were modest and have been in decline for decades, which is why the island has worked hard to build up finance, aluminium and tourism. Walk around Royal Mound 15 and you see both eras at once: the tomb of a Bronze Age elite and the housing blocks of an oil-age middle class.

The mound is one of the group at A'ali, built about four thousand years ago, and today it stands on the edge of Madinat Isa's suburbs. A fence protects it, a low path runs around it, and a small sign explains the site in Arabic and English. Despite the proximity of houses, the setting is quiet, particularly in the early morning when the only traffic is a delivery van or a school bus.

Riders will find it easy to reach. Main roads are good, but the side streets around Madinat Isa are narrow, with parked cars and speed humps, and unmarked humps can be vicious for a loaded bike. Slow down at junctions, as the local habit of reversing out of driveways without looking can be alarming. Keep a close eye on the roundabouts, where the right of way is more theoretical than real.

If you want to follow the oil story, head south to Jebel Dukhan, the low hill at the heart of the field, and visit the Bahrain Oil Museum nearby, which preserves the first well. The Tree of Life stands nearby in the desert, and the ride takes about half an hour on good, straight roads.

Fuel is available all over the island, and Bahraini petrol is among the cheapest in the world. Fill up at any station, as the quality is consistent and most are open late.
t.royal mound 6@26.2,50.5:
A'ali is not only a graveyard. The village that gives the cemetery its name has for generations been the pottery town of Bahrain, and a few workshops still shape red clay on the wheel and fire it in kilns, much as potters did here centuries ago. The big domed jars and incense burners are not antiques but fresh work, and the craftsmen are usually happy to let visitors watch as they turn a lump of wet clay into a perfect curve. The pottery tradition continues despite the arrival of cheap factory ware, and it provides a pleasant link between the ancient tombs and the present.

Royal Mound 6 stands a short ride from the potteries, in the broad plateau of the royal cemetery. It is one of the group built in the early second millennium BC, a monument of stacked limestone with a chamber at its core, and it has been protected by fences since the Danish excavations of the 1950s and later work by Bahraini and international teams. The UNESCO listing in 2019 recognised the area as a landscape of burial that is one of the largest in the world, with thousands of smaller mounds spread across the island.

For a rider, the landscape is easy. Roads between the mounds and the village are flat and wide, with intermittent sand and the occasional pothole where roadworks have been patched. Take care around the village's narrow lanes, where children play and cars park on both sides. Be ready for long waits at junctions in rush hour, and expect to share the road with large trucks carrying construction material, a constant in a country that is always building.

Madinat Isa and A'ali have plenty of shops, and a few small grocery stores sell cold drinks and snacks until late at night. Petrol stations are easy to find, and there is no problem with range.

Ask a potter for a small clay lamp or cup: the price is modest, and it is a better souvenir than anything in a mall.
t.pair of royal mounds 11 and 12@26.2,50.5:
Visitors to Bahrain tend to know two things: the Formula One race and the heat. The Bahrain International Circuit at Sakhir, a short ride south of these mounds, hosted the first Formula One grand prix in the Middle East in 2004 and has been a fixture on the calendar ever since. The pair of Royal Mounds 11 and 12, with their rounded humps and silent faces, offer a startling contrast to the roar of engines. Four thousand years before anyone dreamed of a motor race, the people who lived here were building monuments meant to outlast any circuit.

The circuit is open for tours and track days at various times, and a ride past the grandstands is a reasonable detour for anyone who enjoys the sport. The desert setting is striking, with the track set in a wide expanse of pale sand and distant hills, and the pit complex rises out of the flat land like a ship. Check the website before going, because access depends on the event schedule.

The mounds themselves are a short ride from Madinat Isa, on the A'ali plateau. They are two of the seventeen or so large royal tombs in the cluster, built roughly four thousand years ago and now part of a World Heritage Site that includes twenty-one separate burial sites across the island. The pair stand close together, with a narrow gap between them, and from the right angle they seem almost to lean toward each other.

On the road, you will find a mix of wide, modern carriageways and older local streets. The main roads are fast and well signed, and speeds are enforced by cameras, so keep an eye on the limits. Roundabouts are frequent, and local drivers use them with enthusiasm. When it rains, which is rare, the roads become dangerously slippery, as oil and dust turn the surface to grease.

Fuel is cheap and available everywhere. Madinat Isa has everything you might need, and Sakhir has a small number of cafes and a visitor centre. Bring water, sunscreen and a sense of humour.
t.patacamaya@-17.2,-67.9:
Patacamaya is a market town on the altiplano, the high plain of Bolivia, at around 3,800 metres on the main road between La Paz and Oruro. It is not a pretty place, and that is part of its character: a straggle of concrete and adobe buildings along the highway, with lorries, minibuses and food stalls clustered at the junction. For motorcyclists it matters because of that junction. Here the road to Chile turns west toward the border at Tambo Quemado and the great volcano Sajama, and anyone heading for that route passes through, with a need for fuel, a meal and a rest.

The altiplano is a vast, cold, treeless plateau lying between two ranges of the Andes. The horizon seems enormous and the sky is a deep blue, with clouds that cast moving shadows over the grass. Llamas and alpacas graze in the fields, tended by Aymara families in bowler hats and layered skirts, and mud-brick houses stand with their backs to the wind. The air is thin and dry, with strong sun in the day and freezing temperatures at night. The effects of altitude are real. Headaches and shortness of breath are common, and a motorcycle runs with less power, so take it slowly and drink plenty of water.

The road itself is paved and generally in good condition, running straight across the plateau with only gentle rises. Wind is the main enemy, and the afternoon gusts can be strong, so a steady grip is needed. Trucks are plentiful and slow. Be careful with dogs and animals on the road, and with the speed bumps at village entrances, which are often unmarked. On the road to Sajama, the landscape becomes ever more striking, as the white cone of Sajama, Bolivia's highest peak at about 6,500 metres, rises in the distance.

Patacamaya is a good place to refuel, since stations are scarce on the way west. Food stalls sell grilled meat, soup, and salteñas, the baked pastries of Bolivia, and street vendors sell coca tea, a traditional remedy for altitude. The Sunday market draws people from the surrounding countryside. Cash is necessary, since cards are rarely accepted. The dry season, from May to October, is the best time to ride, although nights are bitterly cold.
t.winter harbor@44.4,-68.1:
Winter Harbor is the real Maine that the postcards approximate: a working lobster village at the end of a long peninsula, with boats at the wharf, stacks of traps in yards and a sign or two selling crabmeat. It sits on the Schoodic Peninsula, the only part of Acadia National Park on the mainland, and the contrast with the busy Mount Desert Island across the bay is huge. Here there are fewer people, more fog and a feeling of being at the edge of the world.

A one-way road of about six miles, it runs around the tip of the peninsula, past pink granite ledges that tumble into the Atlantic, and the waves on a rough day send spray high above the rocks. At Schoodic Point you can walk out on the rock and watch the surf break, with sea ducks bobbing offshore and the long profile of Mount Desert across the bay. The peninsula was once home to a naval base, now an institute for research and education, whose tidy buildings sit among the spruce.

Narrow, twisting and often damp, it has patches of sand and broken edges, and it is shared with cyclists and walkers, so a slow, relaxed pace is the only sensible one. Fog can sweep in and hide everything in minutes, so a clear day is a gift.
