Winter Harbor has a store and a couple of places to eat, including a lobster pound or two in season, but Ellsworth, about thirty kilometers away, is the place for a full tank and a proper supermarket. The best months are June and September, with clear days, and fall color arrives in October, blending red maple with dark spruce. July and August bring the visitors and the traffic, but the loop road absorbs them well. Winter is bleak and quiet, and the loop is partly closed to vehicles.
t.camden@44.2,-69.1:
Camden is the harbor town that makes Maine look as good as it does in the brochures. The Camden Hills rise right behind the town, with Mount Battie, about eight hundred feet high, standing over the inner harbor, and Penobscot Bay lies in front, dotted with islands and sailing vessels. Windjammers, the old-style schooners that take passengers on multi-day cruises, fill the waterfront in summer, their masts and rigging a forest against the sky.

The poet Edna St. Vincent Millay grew up here and wrote her first famous poem, Renascence, after climbing Mount Battie, and a memorial on the summit recalls her. The 1957 film Peyton Place was shot in Camden, which gives the town a small footnote in film history. A road runs to the summit of Battie through Camden Hills State Park, and the view from the stone tower is one of the best on the coast, with the whole harbor, the bay and the islands spread below. The little stream that tumbles through the center of town drops over falls into the harbor, an unusual feature that gives the place charm.

Route 1 is the spine of the coast and the main road through Camden, with traffic that can be slow in summer. Route 52 runs around Megunticook Lake, with gentle curves and glimpses of water, and a little north, Lincolnville Beach has a ferry to Islesboro. South, the road to Rockport and Rockland leads past a quieter harbor and a lighthouse-filled shoreline. Weekday mornings are the time to ride; on summer weekends the main road is a slow procession of cars and rental bikes.

Camden has fuel, markets and enough restaurants for any appetite, from lobster shacks on the wharf to fancier dining rooms. Rockland, about twelve kilometers south, is bigger and has more of everything. The best months are June and September, when the crowds have thinned and the light is soft, and early October brings color to the hills. In July and August the town is delightful but packed. Fog is common in late spring and early summer, and it can shroud the harbor in the morning, so a bit of patience pays off.
t.damariscotta@44.0,-69.5:
Damariscotta is oyster country, and it has been for a very long time. Along the banks of the Damariscotta River, huge heaps of discarded oyster shells, some of them thirty feet deep, mark the places where Native peoples feasted for over two thousand years, and these middens are among the largest on the Atlantic coast. Today the river is home to a thriving aquaculture industry, and the oysters are among the best in the country, served on the half shell in a half-dozen restaurants.

The town sits at the head of a long tidal river, with its twin, Newcastle, across the bridge, and the two share a handsome brick main street that is lively without being touristy. Every October the community holds a Pumpkinfest, with giant pumpkins hauled to the river for a regatta in which people paddle hollowed-out hulls, a sight that draws crowds from all over the state. The old churches and brick buildings give the town the feel of a prosperous nineteenth-century port, which it was.

The ride south from here is one of the best on the coast. Route 130 runs down the Pemaquid Peninsula, with gentle curves, marsh views and glimpses of tidal coves, to Pemaquid Point, where a white lighthouse built in 1827 stands on striking ledges of folded rock. The lighthouse is on the Maine state quarter, and the rocks below it, ribbed and swept by waves, are a fine place to watch the surf. Nearby, the colonial settlement of Pemaquid has an old fort and a museum, a reminder that Europeans were fishing and trading here by the early seventeenth century.

Damariscotta has fuel and a good range of restaurants, bakeries and shops, and it is the main service town for the peninsula. Bigger towns, including Brunswick and Bath, are farther along Route 1. The best months are June and September, when the crowds are gentle and the air is clear, and the October pumpkin festival brings color and noise. July and August are busy, with summer visitors filling every lane. Fog can roll in suddenly on the coast, so dress in layers, and keep an eye out for deer at dusk along the wooded lanes.
t.sand beach@44.3,-68.2:
Sand Beach is the only real sandy beach on Mount Desert Island, and it is a small one, a curve of pale sand tucked between granite cliffs, about 290 metres long. The sand is made largely of crushed shells and the skeletons of sea urchins and other creatures, ground fine by the waves, rather than the quartz you would find on a beach farther south. The water is cold even in August, rarely warmer than the mid-teens in Celsius, which discourages most swimmers beyond the brave and the foolish. Behind the beach, the peaks of Champlain and Huguenot Head rise in a long ridge of pink granite and spruce.

The Park Loop Road leads to it, a twenty-seven-mile circuit around the eastern half of Acadia National Park, with sections that run one-way along the coast. It is a lovely ride, slow and curving, with the Atlantic constantly in sight, and the road passes through spruce forest, past granite headlands and along the rocky shoreline. The speed limit is low, and rightly so, because cyclists and pedestrians share the corners. Summer weekends are crowded, and the car park at Sand Beach is often full by mid-morning, but in September, after the school holidays, and in October with the leaves turning, the park is quieter and the light is exquisite.

Acadia was the first national park east of the Mississippi, created in 1916 as a national monument and renamed in 1929, largely through the efforts of wealthy summer residents, including the Rockefeller family, who built the network of carriage roads that still wind through the woods. The thunder hole nearby is a rock cleft where waves boom and spray in rough weather, best an hour or two before high tide on a stormy day. The fog, which rolls in off the Gulf of Maine in summer, can cut visibility to a few metres, and it brings damp roads and a sharp, salty chill.

Bar Harbor, about six kilometres to the north, is the main town, with petrol, restaurants, ice cream and lobster in unfair quantities. Ellsworth, on the mainland, has bigger supermarkets and more services. The park charges an entrance fee, and parking is limited, so arrive early. Bring a windproof layer, and if you swim, expect to be quick about it. The cliff path from the beach to Otter Point is a lovely walk if you have the time.
t.otter point@44.3,-68.2:
Pink granite meets the Atlantic at Otter Point, and the sea has not yet won. The cliffs here, known as Otter Cliffs, rise about a hundred feet straight out of the water, among the highest headlands on the Atlantic coast between Maine and Rio de Janeiro, and the Park Loop Road runs along their top through a thin screen of spruce. Below, the waves work at the base of the rock with a constant, hollow thud, and the spray hangs in the air on a windy day.

The ride is short but memorable. From Sand Beach, the one-way Park Loop Road follows the shore for a couple of miles, past Thunder Hole and Monument Cove, and the curves are gentle and the speed limit low, so the pace is a slow, scenic crawl. The road is narrow, with granite boulders beside it, and tourists on foot and on bicycles share the shoulder. Going early is the sensible policy, and so is going after Labour Day, when the crowds thin and the light turns clear and golden. In fog, which is common, the cliffs vanish and the foghorn can be heard offshore.

The point itself is a good place to watch. Eiders and guillemots bob in the surf, and in autumn migrating birds pass in numbers. Seals sometimes haul out on the ledges at low tide, and porpoises and the occasional whale can be seen offshore. The rock is the same Cadillac granite that forms the island's mountains, with pale pink feldspar. Rock climbers use the cliffs, so you might see ropes and helmets. The tide pools below are full of periwinkles, barnacles and starfish, though the rocks are slippery and the waves unpredictable.

The Wabanaki, the people of the dawn, lived and fished on this coast for thousands of years before Europeans arrived, and the French navigator Samuel de Champlain named the island in 1604, calling it the isle of bare mountains. The name has been mangled in English as Mount Desert, and locals pronounce the second word like dessert, which tells you something about how language drifts.

Fuel and food are in Bar Harbor, about nine kilometres away, and Ellsworth on the mainland has more. Parking at the point is limited and in summer fills early, but the view is worth the wait.
t.cadillac mountain@44.4,-68.2:
At 466 metres, Cadillac Mountain is the highest point on the US Atlantic coast north of Brazil, and its bare granite summit is the first place in the country to see the sunrise for part of the year, a distinction that has turned a quiet hill into a pilgrimage. The summit is a bald dome of pink rock, scoured by glaciers and polished by wind, and the view from it takes in the whole of Mount Desert Island, the islands of Frenchman Bay, and the blue sweep of the Gulf of Maine. On a clear day, from the right spot, you feel like you can see the curve of the earth.

The road to the top, Cadillac Summit Road, is about three and a half miles of steady climbing from the Park Loop Road, with a smooth surface, a number of pull-outs, and wide, easy bends through scrubby pitch pine and blueberry. It is a favourite with riders, though in season a vehicle reservation is needed, which sells out quickly for sunrise, so check the park website before you plan. Weather matters, because the summit is exposed to wind and fog, and the temperature can be ten degrees cooler than on the shore. The road closes in winter.

The mountain was called Green Mountain until 1918, when it was renamed for Antoine de la Mothe Cadillac, the French adventurer who was granted the island by Louis XIV and later founded Detroit. The car company later borrowed his name. It was one of the early places protected by wealthy summer residents, who set up the land trust that grew into Acadia National Park. Blueberries and cranberries grow in the cracks, and in September, hawks pass overhead in their autumn migration.

Weather and light are the reasons to go, and the best moments are before sunrise or at dusk. In summer the crowds are thick at midday and the car park can be crowded. Walk the loop trail around the top, wear a layer, and take care on the granite, which is slippery when wet. The cairns mark the path.

Bar Harbor, about four kilometres away, has petrol, cafes and shops, and it is the sensible base. Ellsworth, further inland, has big supermarkets. There are no services at the top apart from a small gift shop, so bring water. If you are on a motorcycle, note that parking is separate and often overfull at busy times, so be patient, and expect to wait.
t.putre@-18.2,-69.6:
Putre is a small Aymara village high in the Andes, at about 3,500 metres above sea level, and it is the gateway to Lauca National Park and the high plateau. The village sits on a green terrace above a deep valley, with stone houses, narrow streets and a small, whitewashed church that dates from the seventeenth century. The surrounding hills are dotted with old agricultural terraces that have been farmed for centuries, and the people here, many of them Aymara, graze llamas and alpacas on the high pastures. After the dry desert of the coast, the green of the fields comes as a shock.

The road up from Arica is a steady climb through desert canyons, past giant cacti and villages tucked into oases, and the change in altitude is the main challenge. The road is generally paved and in reasonable condition, with long bends and some sections of steep gradient, and the traffic is light apart from the lorries heading for Bolivia. Be prepared for altitude effects, including headaches, shortness of breath and a loss of engine power, and take your time. Many travellers spend a night in Putre to acclimatise before going higher.

Putre has a few guesthouses, cafes and small shops, and the food is hearty and warming: soups, grilled alpaca and quinoa dishes, with coca tea as the local remedy for altitude. Fuel supplies are limited, so fill the tank in Arica before the climb, and check what is available if you plan to go on to the lake. Nights are cold, even in summer, so bring warm clothing and a sleeping bag if you can.

The landscape beyond is the Altiplano, a high, windswept plateau of grass, lakes and volcanoes, and the wildlife here is a joy to see. Vicuñas graze beside the road, flamingos feed in the shallow lakes, and with luck you will spot a viscacha, a rabbit-like rodent that sits on the rocks. The volcanoes of the Chilean-Bolivian border, with their perfect, snow-dusted cones, fill the horizon, and the air is clear and thin. It is one of the finest high-altitude landscapes in South America, and Putre is a gentle introduction.
t.lake chungara@-18.2,-69.2:
Lake Chungará lies at about 4,500 metres on the Chilean Altiplano, close to the Bolivian border, and it is one of the highest lakes in the world. The water is deep blue, the shore is fringed with pale grass and the sky seems very close. Behind it rise the twin volcanoes of Parinacota and Pomerape, both over six thousand metres, their cones white against the dark blue, and the sight of Parinacota reflected in the still water of the lake is one of the best-known images in the Andes.

The lake was formed when a huge landslide from the volcano dammed a river valley thousands of years ago, creating a natural reservoir that now shelters a rich variety of birds. Flamingos, giant coots, Andean geese and many other species gather on the shore, while vicuñas graze on the slopes and the occasional fox moves through the grass. The protected area around it, Lauca National Park, is a biosphere reserve and a haven for wildlife, and you can often watch animals from the road without leaving your bike.

At this height, the air holds about half the oxygen it does at sea level, and engines lose a great deal of power, so expect your bike to feel sluggish. Riders may notice headaches or breathlessness, so go slowly and avoid heavy exertion. Fill the tank in Arica or Putre and carry warm layers, a windproof jacket and water. Nights fall far below freezing, so do not plan to stay unless you are prepared. Take a moment at the viewpoint, breathe slowly, and look at the mountain in the water. In the thin, clear air, even a short stop feels like an event, and the silence is so complete that you can hear the wind move through the grass.
t.puno@-15.8,-70.0:
Puno stands on the shore of Lake Titicaca at about 3,800 metres, and it is the capital of the Peruvian side of the lake and of Andean folk culture. It is a city of about 116,000 people, a bustling, cold, windswept place with a cathedral in baroque style, a busy port and streets that climb steeply from the water. It began in the seventeenth century as a silver-mining town, and the colonial wealth is visible in the stonework of the churches. Titicaca is the highest navigable lake in the world and one of the largest in South America, and its water is a deep, cold blue under a sky that seems to be closer than it should be. Out on the water, the Uros people live on floating islands made of totora reeds, which they renew constantly, and the island of Taquile is known for its knitted textiles. Boats leave from the harbour in Puno for both, and a day on the water is an essential part of any visit.
