Try the trout from the lake, grilled or fried, and quinoa soup, which is warming in the cold. Altitude is the main concern, and visitors arriving from the coast often feel its effects, so drink plenty of water and move slowly.

The ride along the lake is an unusual one, flat and open, with views of the water and fields of potatoes and quinoa. The road is paved and mostly good, with some rough patches, and the wind off the lake is cold and strong. Mornings are bright, with frost on the ground in winter, and the dry season from May to October is best. Atuncolla, a village about twenty-two kilometres away, stands close to Sillustani, where tall stone burial towers, built by the Colla people before the Incas, stand on a peninsula in a lake. It is an eerie, beautiful place to end a day.
t.chucuito@-15.9,-69.9:
Chucuito is a quiet lakeside town about fifteen kilometres south of Puno, on the shore of Lake Titicaca, and it was once the capital of the Lupaca, a powerful Aymara kingdom that ruled this part of the Altiplano before the Incas. The town has a colonial centre with a neat plaza, stone houses and two fine churches, and the low hills behind it are patched with fields of potatoes and quinoa. The lake is only a short walk away, a vast sheet of dark blue water stretching toward distant mountains.

The town is best known for the Inca Uyo, a walled enclosure with stone phalluses of various sizes, often described as a temple of fertility, which has become an unlikely tourist attraction. Scholars disagree about its origin and purpose, but the place is intriguing, and local guides are happy to tell you their version of the story. The churches, built in the colonial period with local stone, hold paintings and carved altars, and are worth a quiet visit.

The ride from Puno is short and pleasant. The road runs along the lakeshore, paved and in good condition, with long, gentle bends and open views over the water. Wind can be strong, and temperatures drop quickly in the evening, so bring a warm jacket even in summer. Traffic is light, although trucks and buses use the road. The best season is the dry months from May to October, when the skies are clear and the light on the lake is spectacular.

There is no need for much planning, since Puno has fuel and every service you could need, and Chucuito itself has a few cafes, small shops and guesthouses. Ilave, about thirty-two kilometres to the south, is a bigger town with additional services. Enjoy a plate of grilled trout by the lake, take a walk around the plaza and watch the herders bring their sheep home. The sound of church bells and the sight of reed boats on the water give the place a timeless quality, and the thin, clear air makes every colour sharper.
t.juli@-16.2,-69.5:
Juli is a small town of about seven thousand people on the southwest shore of Lake Titicaca, and it carries the nickname Rome of the Andes because of its four colonial churches, some of the grandest in the Altiplano. In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the Jesuits made Juli a centre of missionary work among the Aymara, and they set up a school and a press that is said to have produced some of the first books printed in South America, including works in Aymara and Quechua. The churches, with their stone facades, bell towers and paintings, are still standing, and they give the town a surprisingly serious, historic feel.

The ride from Puno, along the lake road, is one of the quiet pleasures of the Peruvian Altiplano. The road is paved and in generally good condition, with long, flowing bends beside the water and wide views over fields and marshes. Traffic is light, with trucks and local buses, and the wind can be cold and strong, especially in the afternoon. The altitude, at nearly 3,850 metres, makes the air thin, and a rider may feel breathless on arrival. Between May and October, the weather is dry and the sky bright.

Juli has fuel, shops, simple restaurants and a few guesthouses, though choices are limited, and Ilave, about twenty-six kilometres to the north, is larger and has more. The food is simple and good, with grilled trout from the lake, quinoa and potato dishes, and strong coffee. A walk around the plaza and a look into the churches is the best way to spend an hour. Bring cash, since cards are less commonly accepted.

The nearby lake is a haven for birds, and flamingos can sometimes be seen in the shallows near Juli, along with coots, ducks and herons. To the south the road continues toward the Bolivian border, with the island of the Sun, Isla del Sol, lying across the water, a sacred place in Inca belief as the birthplace of the sun. The light on the lake in the late afternoon, when the water turns copper and the mountains of Bolivia glow in the distance, is one of the best sights of the whole Altiplano.
t.copacabana@-16.2,-69.1:
Copacabana is a pilgrimage town first and a lake resort second, and it still carries both jobs without fuss. It sits on the Bolivian shore of Lake Titicaca, at close to 3,800 metres, on a neck of land between two bays and with the Peruvian border post a short hop away; Yunguyo, the Peruvian town just across the line, is the nearest place of any size. Out on the water lies the Isla del Sol, the legendary birthplace of the Inca sun, with the village of Yumani on its southern ridge.

The way in from La Paz is half of the experience. You run north-west over the flat altiplano with the Cordillera Real standing white on your right, then drop toward the lake and arrive at the Strait of Tiquina, where the road simply ends at water. Vehicles cross on small wooden barges, and a bike usually rides along with a truck or a bus on the same raft while the passengers take a launch. Pay the small fee, ride on when told, tie up nothing, and leave the engine off. On the far side the road climbs through eucalyptus and terraced barley to a view over blue water that is hard to believe at this altitude.

The faith is the thing to understand. The Virgen de Copacabana, a dark, carved figure from the late sixteenth century, lives in the white Moorish-looking basilica above the main street, and on weekends owners bring their cars, buses and now motorbikes to be blessed with flowers, beer and firecrackers outside. If you are riding something with an engine, you are expected to take part. It is a cheerful, noisy ceremony and nobody minds a foreigner holding a camera, as long as you ask.

Eat the trout, which comes from the lake, fried or grilled, at the stalls along the waterfront. Nights are cold even when days are sunny, so pack accordingly, and the thin air makes the first evening feel like a long walk after a hard day. The town has fuel stations, but supplies in Bolivia can be uneven and foreign-plated vehicles are sometimes asked for a different price, so top up in La Paz and ask locally. Climb the Calvario hill at sunset for the lake in full colour and a very good reason to have come.
t.tambo quemado@-18.3,-69.0:
Tambo Quemado is not a town so much as a border and a very long queue of trucks. It marks the crossing from Bolivia into Chile on the high road between La Paz and the Pacific coast at Arica, and the altitude, around 4,600 metres, is what everyone remembers, not the paperwork. The name means burnt inn, which tells you it has been a stopping point for travellers for a long time, though the modern place is a cluster of customs buildings, canteens and parked lorries on the open altiplano.

What makes it worth the ride is what surrounds it. The road from the east passes through the Sajama National Park, where the Nevado Sajama rises to 6,542 metres as Bolivia's highest mountain, a perfect, lonely cone that dominates the horizon for an hour before you reach it. Beside it stand the twin volcanoes Parinacota and Pomerape, and beyond the border on the Chilean side is Lago Chungará, one of the highest lakes on Earth, with flamingos, vicuñas and the symmetrical snowcap of Parinacota reflected in it on still mornings. Queñua trees, said to be among the highest forests in the world, cling to the slopes of Sajama.

The riding is long, empty and exposed. The paved road has few bends, but the wind builds from late morning and can push a bike sideways, so try to be moving early and plan to finish before the afternoon gusts. Nights are far below freezing. Expect heavy lorry traffic through the border zone, especially on weekdays, and be ready for long waits on either side. Border formalities, especially for a foreign motorbike, need time, patience and the right papers, so check what you must carry before you set out, since the rules change.

Practicalities are thin up here. There are no towns near the crossing itself, so fill the tank well before: the sensible places are in Patacamaya or the other towns along the road from La Paz, or in Arica on the Chilean side. Sajama village has basic lodging and hot springs nearby, which are just what a rider with frozen fingers wants. Carry water, a warm layer you do not mind getting dusty, and some patience for altitude.
t.oruro@-18.0,-67.1:
Oruro would never win a beauty contest, and its people would be the first to grin about it, but it holds one of the best parties in South America. This is a mining city on the high Bolivian plain, at about 3,700 metres, cold in the evenings and dry the rest of the time, built on tin and silver and still marked by the headframes and slag heaps that gave it money for a century. The nearest settlement of note is the city itself; beyond it the plain runs flat toward the old lake basin of Poopó.

Every year before Lent the city turns into a carnival that UNESCO recognised as a masterpiece of the intangible heritage of humanity. Thousands of dancers in elaborate costumes and enormous masks perform the Diablada, the dance of the devils, up the streets to the Sanctuary of the Virgen del Socavón, the Virgin of the Mineshaft, who is the patron of the miners. The story behind it blends Andean beliefs about the underworld with Catholic saints, and the result is more heartfelt than any parade you have seen. If your dates are flexible, plan for it, though book rooms months ahead and expect closed roads.

For a rider, Oruro is the hinge between La Paz and the south. The highway from La Paz arrives fast and flat across the plateau, and the road south toward Uyuni runs on over the altiplano through Challapata and past the Salar. Between towns there is room, a lot of wind, and almost nothing else, so the day goes in long, quiet pulls with snow-capped volcanoes drifting in and out of view. Mid-morning is best for light and warmth. Afternoons can bring dust and a crosswind that makes the bike lean.

This is a proper city, so fuel, mechanics, and hot food are easy to find, and it is the right place to top up everything before the empty miles to the south. Try the local market stalls for a bowl of thick soup and fried chicken, or the rostro asado, a pig's head dish that locals swear by if you are brave. Keep an eye on your gear in the busy streets, as in any large town, and check the weather forecast for your next leg before committing to a long day.
t.sucre@-19.0,-65.3:
Sucre is the city you stay longer in than you meant to. It is Bolivia's constitutional capital, tucked into a mild valley at roughly 2,800 metres, and its centre is a calm grid of whitewashed colonial buildings with red-tiled roofs that earned it a place on the UNESCO list. The altitude is gentler than La Paz or Potosí, the air is warmer and the pace slower, which is why overlanders tend to rest here after weeks on the plateau.

The city's story is the story of the country. It was founded in the sixteenth century as La Plata, the administrative and legal heart of the silver empire that grew up around nearby Potosí, and it has since carried several names, including Chuquisaca. In 1809 it saw one of the first cries for independence in Spanish America, and in 1825 the declaration of independence was signed in the house now known as the Casa de la Libertad, which is worth an hour. Students fill the streets because of its very old university, which gives the cafés an easy energy.

The riding out of Sucre is better than the city suggests. Roads wind up through eucalyptus-lined hills and dry mountain farmland toward Tarabuco to the east and toward Potosí to the west, with plenty of curves, changes in elevation and occasional wandering livestock. The pavement is serviceable on the main routes and gets rougher on the secondary ones, and the weather can turn quickly from sunshine to rain in the afternoon. Morning light on the white walls and the green hills is the picture to wait for. Plan to be in the saddle before the heat builds.

Since this is a city of a couple of hundred thousand people, fuel, food, repair shops and a good night's sleep are all in easy reach. Eat chorizo chuquisaqueño and drink a cup of hot chocolate from one of the local shops, because Sucre has long made chocolate and takes pride in it. Park the bike securely, since the centre's narrow streets are quiet at night but not unwatched, and give yourself a full day to wander before riding on to the rest of the highlands.
t.potosi@-19.6,-65.8:
Potosí is the highest large city in the world, near 4,000 metres, and it is a place of enormous history. Above it stands the Cerro Rico, the Rich Hill, a reddish cone that gave the Spanish crown so much silver after 1545 that it helped shape the economy of the whole of Europe. For a time Potosí was one of the biggest cities in the world, and the phrase worth a Potosí became a Spanish byword for great wealth. Today the mountain is hollowed out by centuries of tunnels, and cooperative miners still work it, in conditions that leave a mark on any visitor.

The cost is the other side of the story. Indigenous labourers and enslaved Africans worked and died in those mines in numbers nobody can state exactly, and walking the old colonial centre, you see the churches, balconies and the Casa Nacional de Moneda, the royal mint, built to turn that metal into coin, with the shadows of that history close behind. UNESCO lists the city for good reason. Tours into the mines are offered by former miners, and they are not for the claustrophobic.

Riding in, you cross the high plateau on long, quiet roads before the city appears under its dark red peak. From Sucre the road climbs and drops through dry mountains, with a handful of good curves and some rough patches, and the thin air takes a little of the engine's power, so do not be surprised if the bike feels sluggish. Mornings are bright and cold, afternoons bring wind and sometimes hail or snow, so dress for a range. Town streets are steep, cobbled in places and narrow, so ride carefully, particularly when wet.

Potosí has all you need, with fuel, restaurants, workshops and lodging in a city of well over a hundred thousand people, with Betanzos, a much smaller town, the nearest place of any size on the road toward Sucre. Try a salteña, the baked pastry stuffed with juicy filling, which locals eat mid-morning with great ceremony, and a warm cup of coca or herbal tea to help with the altitude. Spend a day before you push on, because the thin air will tire you faster than the road does.
t.cochabamba@-17.4,-66.2:
Cochabamba lies in a broad, warm valley at around 2,550 metres, and the climate is what the locals brag about first: dry, sunny, and mild for most of the year, which earned it the name City of Eternal Spring. It is Bolivia's food capital, a city of nearly a million people if you count the whole urban area, spreading across the valley floor with the Tunari range rising behind it.

The Cristo de la Concordia is the landmark you will see from everywhere, a statue of Christ on a hilltop above the city that is taller than the more famous one in Rio, and you can drive or climb to it for a view over the whole valley. The city also has a stubborn political history. In 2000, residents rose against the privatisation of the water supply in what became known as the Cochabamba Water War, an event that echoed far beyond Bolivia. People here are proud of their independence.

Food is the reason to linger. Try silpancho, a thin breaded steak on rice and potatoes with an egg on top, or chicharrón, fried pork with hominy, and wash it down with chicha, the maize beer of the valley, for which the region is famous. La Cancha, the enormous open-air market on the south side of town, sells almost everything under the sun and is a sensory experience in its own right, though keep your belongings close.

For riders, Cochabamba is a launch pad. Heading west toward Oruro, the road climbs to the high plateau; heading east, toward Santa Cruz, it dives into the Chapare lowlands; and south it runs into valleys with excellent riding toward Torotoro. Traffic in the city itself is dense and sometimes chaotic, with minibuses stopping anywhere, so the best approach is to enter early and leave early. Tiquipaya and Sacaba, the neighbouring towns, are bigger than most places you will have crossed in days.

There is no problem with fuel, repairs, accommodation or anything else, since Cochabamba has everything a major city offers, and it is the best place for service before the rural roads. After weeks at altitude, the valley's thicker air is a welcome change for both rider and engine.
t.torotoro@-18.1,-65.8:
Torotoro is one of those places where the road ends and the real attraction begins. The national park lies in the highlands south-east of Cochabamba, in a landscape of red cliffs, narrow canyons and cave systems carved into folded limestone and sandstone, and the village, a small, quiet place with a plaza and a handful of guesthouses, sits at its edge. There is no larger town close by, so everything you need has to come with you or be found in the village.

What draws people here is time. The rocks hold tracks left by dinosaurs, including large, clearly visible footprints on sloping slabs that were once the muddy shore of an ancient sea, and fossils appear in the cliffs. A guide will take you to see them, as well as the Umajalanta cave, where a short guided walk goes into a cool chamber with underground streams and strange formations. The canyon of El Vergel, a deep gorge with a waterfall at the end, is among the nicest short hikes in Bolivia, and the Ciudad de Itas, a labyrinth of rock, is another stop.

The ride has changed over the years. Once a rough day-long track, parts of the road from Cochabamba have been improved, but conditions still vary and landslides or rain can make some sections difficult, so ask locally before you commit. The scenery is lovely: terraced hillsides, small farms, eucalyptus, dry river valleys, and then, as you climb, a wide view over the folded ranges. Go in the dry season, from about May to October, for better surfaces and clear skies, and aim to arrive before dark, because night riding here is not wise.

Fuel is the main thing to plan. The village is small and I would not rely on a pump, so fill the tank in Cochabamba, carry a spare if your bike has a short range, and ride conservatively. Basic meals and simple rooms are available in the village, often at family-run places, and the nights can be cold. Bring cash, since there are few ways to pay by card. The stars at night, far from any city lights, make it worth staying overnight.
t.segment arbolera parcco chua chua@-16.4,:
At close to four thousand metres, on the Peruvian shore of Lake Titicaca, the air is thin enough that walking briskly feels like work and the light is so sharp it seems to sharpen the edges of everything. This stretch belongs to the Qhapaq Ñan, the great Andean road network that the Inca built and extended across their empire, and here it runs through Aymara farming country between the towns of Yunguyo and Desaguadero, both about twenty kilometres away, with the Bolivian border a short distance east.

There is not much to see of the road at first glance: a line of stones, a raised path through fields of potatoes, quinoa and broad beans, perhaps a low wall. That modesty is the point. The Inca road was a working network of runners, llama caravans and armies, and in places like this it still serves the same villages it always did. Long before the Inca, the region was the heartland of Tiwanaku, whose ceremonial city lies just over the border in Bolivia, and the lake itself remains sacred to the people around it.

Riding at this altitude asks things of both rider and machine. Older carburettor bikes lose noticeable power and may run rich, and you will feel the cold in your hands as soon as the sun drops behind cloud. The paved road along the lake between Puno, Yunguyo and Desaguadero is mostly straight with sudden speed bumps in every village, plus dogs, sheep, minibuses and three-wheel mototaxis. Desaguadero is a busy, chaotic border town; crossing to Bolivia there takes patience and paperwork for the bike. The dry season from about May to September brings blue skies and freezing nights, while summer afternoons often deliver hail and lightning.

Fuel is available in Yunguyo and Desaguadero, but quality can vary, so fill at busy stations. Eat trout from the lake, quinoa soup and hot coca tea, which really does help with the altitude, and keep water and snacks handy. If your head pounds, take it slow; nothing out here rewards hurrying.
t.segment pomata chaca chaca@-16.3,-69.3:
On the southern shore of Lake Titicaca, between Juli and the Bolivian border, the Inca road ran along the edge of the lake at nearly four thousand metres, linking Cusco with the lands of Collasuyu, the southern quarter of the empire. The Pomata section of the Qhapaq Ñan, part of the World Heritage listing of the Inca road system, follows the shore through Aymara villages, terraced hills and fields of potatoes, quinoa and broad beans, with the immense blue lake always beside you. The light at this altitude is intense, the air thin and dry, and the lake changes colour with every passing cloud.

Pomata itself is crowned by the church of Santiago Apóstol, built by the Dominicans in the eighteenth century in the Andean baroque style, with a façade of pink stone carved with plants, fruits and animals by indigenous craftsmen, and windows of thin alabaster that filter the light inside. Juli, a little further west, is known as the little Rome of the Andes for its many colonial churches, and the whole southern shore of the lake is dotted with them, signs of the importance of this region in the colonial period. The Aymara people of the area keep their language and many traditions, and the markets are colourful and lively.

The main road from Puno to Desaguadero, the PE-3S, follows the lakeshore and passes through Juli and Pomata. It is asphalted and generally in good condition, with long, open curves and views of the lake, but trucks heading to and from the Bolivian border are frequent, and in villages, people, dogs, sheep and llamas can be on the road. The altitude affects both riders and engines, and you need time to acclimatise before riding hard. Afternoon winds over the altiplano can be strong, and nights are very cold, often below freezing in the dry season.

Yunguyo, about twenty kilometres away, is the town at the junction for the border crossing to Copacabana in Bolivia, and it has fuel, shops and simple restaurants, as do Juli and Pomata. Try fresh trout from the lake, served fried or grilled, and quinoa soup. Coca tea is widely available and helps with the altitude. If you have time, take a boat from Copacabana to the Island of the Sun, sacred in Inca mythology.
t.bu mahir seashore@26.2,50.6:
Bahrain was once a pearl island, and its fortune depended on a harvest that took place under water. For centuries before oil, the men of Muharraq sailed out into the Gulf in the summer months to dive for oysters, going down on a single breath with a nose clip and a stone to carry them to the bottom, and bringing up baskets of shells in the hope of finding a pearl. The Bahraini pearls were famous, and their trade supported merchants, boat owners and whole districts. In the 1930s the Japanese invented cultured pearls, and the market collapsed, which is partly why Bahrain was so ready for oil.

The seashore at Bū Māhir is on the southern tip of Muharraq island, and it was the starting point for some of the pearling voyages, with a fort, a pier and a view across the water. It is part of a trail of buildings and sites in Muharraq, which UNESCO listed in 2012 as a testimony to the island's pearling economy, including merchants' houses, shops and a mosque. The old town of Muharraq, with its narrow lanes, coral-stone houses and wind towers, is a quiet and rewarding place to wander, and some of the houses have been restored.

Bahrain is tiny, flat and well connected, so a ride here is easy. The King Fahd Causeway links the island to Saudi Arabia, and the roads on the island are wide, smooth and busy, with fast traffic and wide junctions. Sakhir, in the south, has the Formula One circuit, and the desert road there is a favourite of local riders. The heat is intense in summer, with humidity too, so the best time to ride is from November to March. A fresh sea breeze at Bū Māhir is welcome, though it may be hazy with dust.

Fuel is plentiful and cheap in Muharraq and nearby Manama, and there are cafes, bakeries and restaurants in the old town. Try the local dates and the Arabic coffee, served with cardamom, and the fish dishes, such as machboos, a spiced rice with fish or meat. Dress modestly in the old town and mosque areas, and be aware that Friday is a quiet day, with many places closed in the morning.
t.core zone 2@26.2,50.5:
Bahrain's pearl-diving history is the reason this scrap of coast matters. For centuries, before oil, the island's wealth came from the oyster beds in the shallow waters, and divers went out for months each summer, working with a nose clip, a stone weight and a basket. Pearls from these waters were prized from India to Europe. Then in the 1930s cultured pearls from Japan collapsed the market, and oil, struck in 1932, took over. The Pearling Path, a UNESCO listing since 2012, preserves buildings and sea sites connected with that older economy, including Fakhro House and the offshore oyster beds called Hayr Shtayyah.

The coordinates here sit on the northern coast, a few kilometres from Jidd Ḩafş and not far from the great mound of Qal'at al-Bahrain, the Dilmun-era fort-tell that is also a World Heritage Site. This is a flat, low landscape of date palms, sandy shoreline and busy suburbs, with the sea glittering just beyond the last buildings. The oyster beds themselves lie out in the water and are not something you ride to, but the shoreline gives you a sense of the old geography.

Riding in Bahrain is straightforward. Roads are good, mostly dual carriageways, with roundabouts and flyovers, and the drivers are fast. Fuel is cheap and available everywhere, and Manama, about seven kilometres away, has everything from cafés to workshops. The King Fahd Causeway links Bahrain to Saudi Arabia, though border formalities are time consuming. Check the rules for entering with a motorcycle before you plan a crossing.

The cooler months from November to March are the time to come, with pleasant days and mild nights. Summer is brutal, with temperatures above forty-five degrees and thick humidity, and a ride in the afternoon is a bad idea. At dusk the call to prayer drifts over the water, and dhows and fishing boats come in as the sky turns orange. Try a Bahraini breakfast of balaleet, sweet vermicelli with eggs, and strong cardamom coffee.
t.segment ccaje sisipampa pomata@-16.2,-69:
Segment Ccaje-Sisipampa-Pomata is a stretch of the Qhapaq Ñan, the great Inca road network, that survives on the high plateau beside Lake Titicaca. The Inca built roads like these across the Andes, stone-paved, with drainage, retaining walls and way stations, to link their empire from Colombia to Chile. On the Peruvian shore near Pomata the road passes through country that was Aymara long before the Incas arrived, and the same communities farm potatoes, quinoa and barley today. The Qhapaq Ñan has been listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site, with sections in six countries.

Pomata is also known for its church of Santiago Apóstol, an eighteenth-century Baroque church of red sandstone sitting on a hill above the lake, carved with Andean motifs that mix Spanish and indigenous design. Juli, about sixteen kilometres away, has a string of old churches and was once called the little Rome of the Andes, while Yunguyo is the bigger town toward the Bolivian border at Copacabana. You will find fuel in both Juli and Yunguyo, but not much in between.

The altitude is the main fact of the ride: the lake sits at about 3,800 metres, so the air is thin, the sun fierce and the nights very cold. Give yourself a day or two to acclimatise, drink plenty of water, and expect your engine to feel a little breathless, too. The road beside the lake is paved, with long, easy bends and views of the water, reed boats and green fields, and the plateau is dotted with adobe houses and grazing alpacas. Wind and hail can arrive without warning in the afternoon.

The dry season, from May to September, brings clear skies, brilliant light and frosty mornings. The rainy season, from December to March, turns the tracks to mud and fills the afternoons with thunder. On the lake you may see the floating reed islands of the Uros, made of totora, though those are closer to Puno. Try trout from the lake, quinoa soup, and a cup of muña tea, which settles the stomach at altitude.
t.persepolis@29.9,52.9:
The staircase at Persepolis is a lesson in how an empire wanted to be seen. Darius I began the terrace in about 518 BC, and his successors added to it for nearly two centuries, building a great ceremonial capital on a platform at the foot of the Mountain of Mercy. Visitors from across the empire climbed the broad, shallow steps to the Gate of All Nations, flanked by huge stone bulls with human heads, and the reliefs of the Apadana, the great audience hall, show delegations from twenty-three subject peoples bringing gifts, Medes, Egyptians, Ethiopians and Indians among them, in a long procession that is still crisp after twenty-five centuries. In 330 BC Alexander the Great captured the city and burned the palace, and the ruined columns that stand today are the remains of that fire.

The scale is what stays with you. The columns of the Apadana were nearly twenty metres high, and they held a cedar roof, and the stone terrace is the size of a small town. Nearby, at Naqsh-e Rostam, the tombs of Darius and his successors are cut into a cliff in the shape of a cross, with Sasanian reliefs below. The site is in the Marvdasht plain, a broad, fertile basin with wheat fields and orchards, with low ridges of pale rock on either side.

Persepolis was listed by UNESCO in 1979, one of the first sites on the list. The best light is in the early morning and late afternoon, when the stone turns golden, and the heat is moderate. Midday in summer is fierce.

The roads of Fars are long and straight across the plains and twist in the hills, with a good surface on the main routes. Traffic is heavy near Shiraz, which has the Bagh-e Eram garden and the tomb of Hafez, and drivers are fast and assertive. Check the rules for foreign visitors and vehicles before you plan. Marvdasht, about ten kilometres from the site, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.segment kallamarka apacheta@-16.6,-68.5:
On the Bolivian altiplano, a few dozen kilometres west of La Paz, the old Inca road runs across a plateau lifted nearly four thousand metres into the sky. This segment of the Qhapaq Ñan is part of the road network that UNESCO recognised in 2014, and it passes near Tiwanaku, the great pre-Inca city whose carved gateways and monoliths stand on the flat plain close to Lake Titicaca. An apacheta is a cairn of stones left by travellers at a pass or a high point, each stone a small offering to the mountain spirits, the apus, and the habit has not died, so you will still find them piled by the roadside, sometimes with coca leaves or a bottle of alcohol beside.

The landscape is huge and treeless, with a pale yellow grass, adobe farms, quinoa fields, herds of llamas and sheep and the white wall of the Cordillera Real on the horizon. Snow peaks like Illimani and Huayna Potosí hang over the plain on clear mornings. The light is hard and bright, and the weather can change rapidly, with hail and thunderstorms in the wet season from December to March.

For riders, the altiplano is wide open and tempting but unforgiving. The main road from La Paz toward Tiwanaku and Desaguadero is paved, with long straight stretches, trucks and speed bumps in villages, while side tracks are dirt and can be soft after rain. Altitude saps your energy, and engines run rich, so a carburetted bike may feel flat. Take time to acclimatise in La Paz or El Alto before riding, drink water, and carry a warm layer, because even in the dry season from May to October the night temperatures drop below freezing.

Tiahuanaco, a town of about three thousand people about eighteen kilometres away, has basic shops, simple restaurants and tiny guesthouses, but fuel supply can be unreliable, so fill up in El Alto or La Paz, where there are many stations and repair shops. Foreign riders may have to show papers at checkpoints, and fuel for foreign-registered vehicles has sometimes been sold at a higher price. Local food includes grilled trout from the lake, potato dishes, and the sweet corn drink called api, served hot in the morning.
t.janabiyah@26.2,50.5:
Bahrain is a small island, but it has been important for a very long time. Under the name Dilmun, it was a trading centre of the Bronze Age, linking Mesopotamia with the Indus valley, and the fresh water that bubbles up from beneath the seabed made it a stop for ships. Janabiyah lies on the western side of the main island, near the coast road, a village among low, flat land where date palms, farms and new housing meet the edge of the desert.

The surrounding area is full of history. Thousands of burial mounds, built by the Dilmun people about four to five thousand years ago, dot the landscape, forming one of the largest ancient cemeteries in the world. Some are low humps, others are large enough to contain chambers, and they appear in unexpected places, between houses and at roadsides. The Bahrain Fort, Qal'at al-Bahrain, on the north coast, is a World Heritage site, and the Tree of Life, a lone mesquite that has survived for centuries in the desert, is a popular curiosity.

Bahrain is also a place for motorsport. The Bahrain International Circuit in the south holds a Formula One race each year, and the island has a strong culture of cars and bikes. The roads are wide, flat and well surfaced, with modern highways linking the main centres, and traffic can be heavy in the evening. Speed cameras are common, and fines are high. The King Fahd Causeway, which links Bahrain to Saudi Arabia, is a few minutes away to the east.

Fuel is cheap and available everywhere, and there are shops and cafes in every village. Madinat Isa, about seven kilometres away, is a large, planned town with every service. The best time to ride is from November to March, when the days are warm and the nights cool, while summer is extremely hot and humid. In the evening, the sea breeze is a relief, and the coastal road toward Bu Mahir and the old pearling coast is pleasant.
t.segment tiwanacu@-16.5,-68.7:
Tiwanaku stands on the Altiplano of Bolivia, at about 3,850 metres, in a bare, cold plain ringed by far mountains. The road you take there passes through the little town of Tiahuanaco, where the colonial church is built partly of stone taken from the ancient ruins, and where the central square holds some of the carved monoliths. This segment is part of the Qhapaq Nan, the Inca road system, which linked the empire from Colombia to Chile and was inscribed by UNESCO in 2014.

The roads of the Incas were built on the foundations of earlier routes, and the people of Tiwanaku, who flourished here between about 500 and 1000 AD, had their own network of tracks and way stations. Llama caravans carried goods from the lowlands and the lake, and the ceremonial centre drew pilgrims from a wide area. The Incas, who arrived later, treated the site with reverence and incorporated its myths into their own, and the ruins stood as a reminder that even their great empire had predecessors.

The landscape is high and harsh. The air is thin, and the sky is deep blue. The wind is cold, even in summer, and in the morning, frost can cover the fields. Farmers grow potatoes and quinoa on the plain, and herds of llamas and sheep graze among them. The Andes, with snow on the high peaks of the Cordillera Real, form a long line on the horizon, and Lake Titicaca lies not far to the north-west.

For a rider, it is an easy ride on a good main road from La Paz, though the altitude makes engines run rich and riders breathless. Fuel is available in Tiahuanaco in small quantities, but it is wise to fill up in El Alto or at larger stations along the highway. The best season is the dry winter, from May to September, with clear days and freezing nights. Bring layers and sun cream, as the sun at this height burns quickly, and drink plenty of water.
t.tiwanaku spiritual and political centre:
Tiwanaku is the most important archaeological site in Bolivia, and standing in the middle of it at nearly 3,900 metres, with the thin air making you light-headed, it is easy to feel why. This was the spiritual and political heart of a civilisation that rose around Lake Titicaca between about 500 and 1000 AD, and at its peak it controlled a territory that reached into modern Peru and Chile. UNESCO inscribed it in 2000.

The main structures are the Akapana, a stepped pyramid that was once faced with stone, the Kalasasaya, a large rectangular platform surrounded by walls, and the Semi-Subterranean Temple, whose walls are studded with stone heads. The Gateway of the Sun, a monolithic arch carved from a single block of andesite, is the best known, with a central figure of a staff-bearing deity surrounded by winged attendants. The stonework is astonishingly precise, with blocks that fit together without mortar, and the Ponce Monolith and the Bennett Monolith are huge carved figures that stand in the courtyards.

The Tiwanaku people farmed the cold plain using raised fields, which protected crops from frost, and built a state that lasted for centuries. Why it collapsed remains a matter of debate, but drought is the leading theory. The Spanish later used many of the stones to build churches and houses, and what survives is only part of what was once there.

The riding is on a good paved highway from La Paz, running across the flat, windswept Altiplano with views of the snowy Cordillera Real. The altitude affects both rider and machine, so go slowly and give yourself time to acclimatise in La Paz first. Fuel is available in El Alto and in Tiahuanaco, though it is best to fill up before leaving the city. The dry winter months, from May to September, are the best, with clear skies, but the nights are freezing. Allow a couple of hours to walk through the site and the museum, and bring a hat, sun cream and warm clothing.
t.sajama@-18.1,-68.9:
Sajama rises alone from the Altiplano, a perfect volcanic cone of 6,542 metres, the highest peak in Bolivia, and the national park that surrounds it, created in 1939, was the first in the country. The mountain stands in the west, near the border with Chile, in a flat, high, windswept country of yellow grass, with twin snowy peaks of Parinacota and Pomerape, on the Chilean side, standing as neighbours. Seen from the road in the clear, thin light, it seems close enough to touch and takes hours to reach.

The land around lies at about four thousand metres, and the altitude affects everything, so spend time acclimatising in La Paz and take it slowly. Nights are very cold, and daytime sun is fierce, with strong ultraviolet and a drying wind. The park is home to vicuñas, the wild relatives of the llama, whose fine wool is among the most valuable in the world, along with rheas, Andean foxes, viscachas and flamingos on the lakes. On the slopes of the volcano grows the queñua forest, one of the highest forests in the world, with twisted trees at over four thousand metres and above.

The village of Sajama is a small cluster of adobe houses, with a church from the colonial era and a number of chullpas, ancient burial towers, standing on the plain. Close by, hot springs bubble at Manasaya and the geyser field at Sajama, a warm bath in the cold dry air after a long ride. Along the way, the church at Curahuara de Carangas, with its painted interior of the seventeenth century, is known as the Sistine Chapel of the Altiplano and is well worth a stop.

The road from La Paz, about two hundred and eighty kilometres, runs across the flat Altiplano, much of it paved, with long straight sections, and a final stretch that may be rough. Wind is constant and can be bitter, and bikes are pushed around. The air is thin and engines lose power, so jetting and fuelling need attention.

Simple lodgings and a campsite serve visitors, and the stars at night are astonishing, in a dark sky with the Milky Way blazing. Pack a thick sleeping bag and a flask.
t.wellfleet@41.9,-70.0:
Wellfleet is a small town on the outer arm of Cape Cod, where the land narrows and the Atlantic is never far away. It has a snug harbour on the bay side, with oyster beds on the flats, and a long, wild coast on the other, where the dunes and beaches of the Cape Cod National Seashore face the open ocean. The oysters here have been famous since the seventeenth century, and the briny, plump Wellfleet oyster is served in restaurants across the country. A plate of them at a harbourside bar, with a cold beer, is the thing to do.

The outer Cape has an unexpected technological history. In 1903, on the cliffs in South Wellfleet, the Italian inventor Guglielmo Marconi built a wireless station with four huge towers, and in January of that year it sent the first transatlantic wireless message from the United States to England, a greeting from President Theodore Roosevelt to King Edward VII. The cliffs have since eroded, and the site is now a small park with a model of the station and a trail to the cliff edge, from which you can see the waves breaking on the long beach far below.

The ocean beaches, with names like Cahoon Hollow and Newcomb Hollow, are wide and wild, backed by high sandy cliffs, with surf that attracts swimmers and surfers. The water is cold, and the undertow can be strong, so take care. The cliffs, made of glacial sand, retreat by a metre or more each year, and the history of shipwrecks along this coast, called the graveyard of the Atlantic, is long. On the bay side, Wellfleet Bay Wildlife Sanctuary has trails through marsh and woods, and a drive-in cinema on the highway has been showing films under the stars since the 1950s.

Route 6 is the main road, busy in summer but a pleasant ride in the shoulder seasons, with pine woods, ponds and glimpses of the sea. Fuel and food are available in Wellfleet and in Eastham, a few kilometres to the south, and there are fried clam shacks, bakeries and seafood restaurants. Fog and wind can be sharp, and the temperature drops at night. September and early October are lovely, with warm water, clear light and few people. Give yourself time to wander on the beach.
t.truro@42.0,-70.0:
Truro is the narrowest part of Cape Cod, where the land is so thin that you can see the ocean on one side and the bay on the other from the same low hill. It is a town of rolling dunes, scrub pine, heath and small cottages, with only a couple of thousand people living here year round, and a quiet that is unusual in this much-visited region. The Cape Cod National Seashore covers much of the town, protecting the dunes, cliffs and beaches, and the sense of space is wonderful.

The place has a great deal of history. In November 1620, the Pilgrims of the Mayflower anchored off the tip of the Cape, and a party went ashore at Truro, where they found a store of buried corn and took it, an act they later regretted and repaid. They stayed only a few weeks before sailing on to Plymouth. Later, the town became a whaling and fishing centre, and Highland Light, the oldest lighthouse on the Cape, built in 1797, stands on a bluff above the sea, a short white tower that has been moved back from the eroding cliff to keep it safe.

Truro has also been an artists' haven. The painter Edward Hopper began spending summers here in the 1930s, and his stark, luminous paintings of sunlit houses and dunes capture the light of the outer Cape, a pale, clear brightness that comes from sea and sand. The landscape has changed little since his time. A small vineyard in the town makes wine from grapes grown in the sandy soil. Down the road, the Pamet River valley is a glacial trough that cuts across the Cape.

Route 6 runs through the middle, a narrow road with a low speed limit and careful enforcement, and the ride is slow and scenic, with dunes, ponds and distant views of the sea. Fuel is not available in the town itself, so fill up at Wellfleet or Eastham or, to the north, in Provincetown, and be aware that services are limited out of season. The air is cooler on the bay side, and the wind can be strong. Summer weekends are crowded, but spring and autumn are quiet and bright. Stay for the sunset over the bay.
t.sieur de monts@44.4,-68.2:
Sieur de Monts is the quiet doorway to the Acadia you came for, a shaded corner of Mount Desert Island with a spring, a nature centre and a small botanical garden. The name comes from Pierre Dugua, Sieur de Monts, the French nobleman who led the expedition that landed on these coasts in 1604 with Samuel de Champlain. The spring was developed by George Dorr, one of the park's founders, who spent decades assembling land and gifting it to the nation. Acadia became the first national park east of the Mississippi in 1916, under the name Lafayette, and took its current name in 1929.

Mount Desert is an island of pink granite, rounded by glaciers and cut with long freshwater lakes and fjord-like inlets. Spruce and fir crowd down to the sea, and the air smells of resin and salt. The Park Loop Road, a twenty-seven mile route that winds around the island, passes right by here, with some sections running one-way, and it is generally smooth and slow, with a modest speed limit and plenty of cyclists and walkers. Think of it as a leisurely tour rather than a performance.

Bar Harbor, the main town, is a short way off and has fuel, food and plenty of lobster. Ellsworth, on the mainland about twenty-six kilometres away, is a bigger town with more shops and gas stations. The park charges an entrance fee, and in the high season some of the busiest places, such as the road up Cadillac Mountain, need a timed reservation, so check the official site beforehand. Summer is crowded, so aim for early morning or late afternoon, or visit in September and October, when the crowds thin and the light turns clear and golden.

Carry a jacket, even in July, because sea fog can roll in without warning and chill the whole island. Carriage roads built by John D. Rockefeller Jr. wind through the woods here, closed to motor vehicles, which gives the place a hush that surprises first-time visitors.
t.jordan pond@44.3,-68.3:
Jordan Pond is one of the loveliest bodies of water in Maine, a deep, clear lake cut by glaciers and ringed with spruce and granite. At the far end two rounded hills called the Bubbles rise like a pair of bumps on the skyline, and the water is so clear that you can see boulders far below the surface. It is a place where rides slow down, because the setting asks for it and because the car park beside the lake is usually busy.

On the lawn above the water, the Jordan Pond House has served tea and popovers since the late nineteenth century, a ritual that visitors still follow. The original building burned in 1979 and was replaced, but the tradition survived, and sitting on the grass with a warm popover and a view of the Bubbles is one of the standard pleasures of the island. In summer the tables fill early and the wait can be long, so go before noon or in mid-afternoon. A walking path circles the lake in about three miles and gives a gentler pace than the road.

Riding to the pond is part of the experience, since the Park Loop Road approaches along the base of the mountains with views through the trees. The road is smooth and carefully engineered, with granite curbs, low stone bridges and a speed limit that discourages heroics. Parts of the loop are one-way, so read the signs. Traffic can be heavy, and cyclists, buses and drivers who are looking at the scenery all need patience.

Fuel is in Bar Harbor, a short run away, and Ellsworth has more. Nothing at the pond sells petrol, only food and souvenirs. October is a favourite time, when the hills turn red and orange and the water is dark and still. Bring a layer, since it can be cool beside the lake even on a warm day, and allow at least an hour.
t.eastham@41.8,-70.0:
Route 6 runs down the length of Cape Cod like a spine, and in Eastham it finally stops pretending to be a highway. The trees get lower and scrubbier, the sky gets bigger, and somewhere around here you realise the land has narrowed to a strip of sand with the Atlantic on one side and Cape Cod Bay on the other. Eastham is the gateway to the Outer Cape, and it has the practical side of that job: a proper town of a few thousand year-round residents, with fuel, groceries and a decent chance of a coffee before you commit to the dunes.

The riding is gentle rather than thrilling. This is a road for rolling along at a relaxed pace, pitch pine and scrub oak crowding both sides, and the real pleasure is in the detours. The side roads toward the ocean side lead to the Cape Cod National Seashore, which protects most of the outer beach from here north to Provincetown. The Salt Pond Visitor Center sits right off Route 6 and is a sensible place to learn what you are looking at. Go early in the morning or on a shoulder-season weekday; in July and August the whole peninsula funnels onto one or two roads and the traffic crawls.

The history here is thick for such a flat place. Eastham was settled by Pilgrims from Plymouth in the 1640s, and the Cape's first explorers reportedly came ashore near here before they settled on Plymouth. The old windmill on the green is among the oldest on the Cape, moved to Eastham in the 1790s. Out on the ocean side, Henry Beston spent a year in a tiny shack on the dunes in the 1920s and wrote The Outermost House about it. The shack was swept away in the great blizzard of 1978, which tells you something about the beach. Nauset Light, the red and white lighthouse people photograph, had to be hauled back from the eroding bluff in the 1990s, and the sea is still taking the cliffs.

The nature is the reason to come. Salt marsh, tidal creeks, cranberry bogs, kettle ponds left by the glaciers, and in the right season a cold, clean smell of salt and bayberry. The Cape Cod Rail Trail also begins nearby, though it is for bicycles. Take the wind seriously on a bike: crosswinds on the open stretches can be stiff, and sand drifts over the lot edges near the beaches, so go slowly on gravel.

For food, the Cape clam shack tradition is alive here, and fried clams, chowder and lobster rolls are the sensible orders. Orleans, a few minutes south, has more of everything if Eastham looks thin.
t.la cumbre@-16.3,-68.0:
La Cumbre is the top of the world's most famous bad road. At about 4,650 metres, on a windswept pass in the Cordillera Real a short ride from La Paz, the tarmac gives way to the old North Yungas Road, which drops from this bare, cold, grey landscape to the steamy green jungle valleys about three and a half thousand metres below. The air is thin enough that a short walk from the bike leaves you breathless, and small roadside shrines hold the offerings that drivers leave for a safe descent.

The road down is the Camino de la Muerte, the Death Road, so named by the Inter-American Development Bank in the 1990s, when it was described as the most dangerous road in the world. The old track, carved into the cliff by Paraguayan prisoners of war in the 1930s, was only a few metres wide, with a drop of hundreds of metres on one side, and by most accounts hundreds of people died every year in crashes. A modern highway opened in 2006 and took most of the traffic, and the old road is now used mainly by cyclists, riders and tour groups. It is still a narrow, gravelled, rutted road with no barriers, and drivers keep to the left so that the driver can see the edge.

For a motorcyclist, the descent is an adventure that demands respect. The gravel is loose, the drops are real, and waterfalls splash across the road in places, making patches of mud. Fog and rain are common and visibility can disappear in seconds. There is a small fee to ride the old road, collected at a checkpoint. Many riders choose to hire a local guide on the first descent, and it is wise to avoid the afternoon when mist comes in, and to give the groups of cyclists plenty of room.

The altitude is a serious matter. La Paz sits at about 3,600 metres and El Alto above it at 4,000, and the ride to La Cumbre adds more. Altitude sickness is real, so spend a day or two acclimatising, drink water, and take it easy. Bikes lose power in thin air and carburetted engines can run rich. The cold and the wind are formidable, and snow is possible even in the dry season, from May to October, which is the best time to ride.

Fuel and services are in La Paz, about twenty-two kilometres away, and there is nothing at the pass. Fill the tank before you leave, bring water and warm gear, and keep an eye on the weather.
t.yolosa@-16.2,-67.7:
Yolosa is the bottom of the Death Road, and the first place where you notice that you have stopped being cold. After hours of descent from the freezing pass, your jacket suddenly feels absurd. The air is warm and wet, the vegetation is thick and loud with insects, and the village sits at the junction where the old road meets the new highway, at about 1,200 metres in the lower Yungas. It is a small, dusty and unpretentious place, and it exists mainly as a crossroads.

The Yungas are the steep, forested valleys where the Andes fall away toward the Amazon basin, and they have been farmed since long before the Spanish arrived. The warm, humid slopes grow coffee, bananas, citrus and coca, and the coca leaf, chewed and brewed as tea, is a legal and traditional crop here, grown on narrow terraces on the hillsides. You will see the bright green bushes drying in the sun on cloths by the road. Near Coroico, the Afro-Bolivian community, descended from enslaved people brought to work in the mines and farms, keeps its own music, dress and a royal family, a fascinating part of Bolivia's history that most visitors miss.

From Yolosa, the road climbs a few kilometres to Coroico, a pleasant hillside town with a plaza, cafes and hotels, and a view back up to the mountains from which you have come. Many riders and cyclists end the day there with a hot shower and a cold beer. The ride on this stretch is easy compared with the descent, with smooth tarmac, long bends and a river down in the valley, but rock falls and landslides can occur in the wet season, from November to March, and the highway is sometimes closed.

At the junction there are stalls, small restaurants and a few places where you can find a simple meal, usually chicken, rice and potatoes with a spicy sauce. I cannot promise fuel at the junction itself, and supplies in Bolivia can be unreliable, so ask in Coroico, three kilometres up the hill, or plan on La Paz for the climb back. If you ride back to the city, the afternoon often brings cloud and rain to the upper road, so start early and carry warm clothing.

The contrast between La Cumbre and Yolosa, from rock and ice to banana palms in a single day, is among the most dramatic in South America.
t.segment paucarcolla yanamayo@-15.8,-70.0:
The Qhapaq Nan is the great road system of the Inca, a web of paths, causeways and stairways that ran for more than thirty thousand kilometres across the Andes, and a stretch near Puno is part of it. The segment between Paucarcolla and Yanamayo follows the plateau around the northwest shore of Lake Titicaca, where the Inca built a road to link the Collao, the great high plain, with the heart of the empire at Cusco. The route is now part of the UNESCO listing of the Andean Road System, which was granted in 2014 and spans six countries.

The altiplano is a landscape of big skies. Lake Titicaca lies at about 3,800 metres, the highest large navigable lake in the world, and its water is a deep, shining blue under a thin, bright atmosphere. Around it, treeless plains are crossed by low hills, with fields of potato, quinoa and barley, herds of alpacas and sheep, and villages of adobe and thatch. Wind is constant, and the sun is fierce, but the nights are bitterly cold. The ride from Puno to Juliaca is easy, with smooth roads and little traffic, though trucks and buses move quickly.

Altitude is the big issue. A rider coming up from the coast or from Cusco will feel the thin air immediately, with headaches, breathlessness and poor sleep, and the engine will run rough, losing power. Spend a night or two in Puno before making any ambitious plans, drink a lot of water, and avoid alcohol on the first evening. Many people find coca tea helpful.

Puno is a decent town for supplies. It has fuel, restaurants, a pleasant waterfront and a lively market. Try trout from the lake, quinoa soup and chuno, freeze-dried potatoes, which the highlanders have prepared for centuries. Atuncolla, the nearby town, lies close to Sillustani, a hilltop site with towering funerary towers, the chullpas, built by the Colla people before the Inca. They are worth a visit for the view over the lake. The Uros, who live on floating islands built of totora reeds, are a short boat trip from Puno.

The best season is from May to October, when the days are dry and sunny. Frost is common on winter mornings, so warm clothing is essential.
t.segment yanamayo kancharani@-15.9,-70.0:
This segment of the Inca road runs just outside Puno, on the western shore of Lake Titicaca, and it connects with a longer line that leads toward the south and the Bolivian frontier. Yanamayo and Kancharani are small places on the Collao plateau, where the road, now often reduced to a stony track, crosses fields and low ridges. The Inca engineers built it to a standard width, with stone edges in places and stone drains, and some stretches are still clearly visible. For an observer used to modern roads, a path built for walkers and llama trains is an eloquent thing. It ran without wheels, since the Inca had no wheeled transport, and was meant to carry foot messengers, armies and caravans of animals.

The surrounding country is classic altiplano. The ground is high and open, with clumps of ichu grass, rounded hills and scattered adobe farmsteads. Cattle and sheep graze among the stubble. A stiff wind blows most afternoons, and thunderstorms roll across the plateau in the wet season, from December to March. Skies at this altitude are extraordinarily clear, and the night stars are dense and bright. Lake Titicaca appears and disappears at the edge of sight, glinting under the clouds.

Puno, only three and a half kilometres away, is the base. The town is built on a slope above the lake, with a cathedral, a main square and a waterfront promenade. Fuel, shops, restaurants and small hotels are plentiful, and the town has an energetic festival culture. The Fiesta de la Candelaria, held in February, is one of the largest folk festivals in South America, with brass bands and dancers in elaborate costumes filling the streets for days. If your trip falls at that time, book accommodation far ahead.

For riding, the road south from Puno along the lake toward Juli, Pomata and Desaguadero is among the finest in the region, with views over the water and the Bolivian mountains beyond. The tarmac is generally good, though sections can be rough, and the border town of Desaguadero is crowded and chaotic. Take it slowly at altitude, and wear layers, since mornings are freezing and afternoons can be warm. May to October is the dry season, with the clearest skies.
t.orleans@41.8,-70.0:
Orleans sits at the elbow of Cape Cod, where the arm of the peninsula bends north into the open Atlantic, and the sense of being at the edge of something begins here. It is a small town of about fifteen hundred year-round residents, with a handful of shops, a pleasant harbour at Rock Harbor and a few miles of beach on either side. The Cape Cod National Seashore, created in 1961 under President Kennedy, begins to the north in Eastham and runs along the outer shore for forty miles, a long line of high dunes, marsh and ocean beach.

The town has an unlikely place in the history of communication. In 1891 a transatlantic telegraph cable from Brest, in France, came ashore here, and the French Cable Station remained in operation for decades. The Nauset Light, a small red-and-white lighthouse a short way north in Eastham, was moved back from an eroding cliff in 1996, a reminder of how quickly the sea is taking the outer coast, which retreats by about a metre or more a year.

On a motorcycle, the Outer Cape is a gentle, unhurried place. Route 6A and the smaller roads are narrow and shaded, with cranberry bogs, saltmarsh and low pine woods, and speeds are slow. The best views are of dunes, ponds and the ocean breaking on wide beaches. Summer traffic is the main issue, since the single road in and out of the Cape is jammed on Friday and Sunday afternoons, with cars crawling for hours at the bridges. An early start or a midweek trip makes all the difference. September and early October are the sweetest months, with warm water, clear light and fewer people.

Fuel is available in Orleans and Eastham, and prices are higher than on the mainland, so it makes sense to fill before crossing the bridges. Seafood is the local pleasure, with fried clams, lobster rolls, oysters from the bay and chowder, and a lobster shack by the water is a good place to rest. The ponds around Wellfleet are a pleasant place for a swim.

Watch for sand on the road near the beaches, and for cyclists, who are common. A walk on the beach at sunset, with the whole Atlantic ahead of you, is a good way to finish the day.
t.doha@25.3,51.5:
Doha is a young city on a flat, dry peninsula, and it grew almost from nothing in a lifetime. Fishing and pearling villages were what the coast held until oil and gas arrived, and in the decades since, the skyline of West Bay has risen along the curve of the harbour like a glass forest. The Corniche, a long waterfront promenade, is the place to see the contrast, with the towers on one side and the traditional wooden dhows drifting on the other. Across from the promenade, the Museum of Islamic Art stands on its own island, a pale, geometric building designed by I. M. Pei and opened in 2008, with collections that reach from Spain to India.

The old part of town centres on Souq Waqif, a market rebuilt in the traditional style, where you can wander lanes of spices, perfumes, falcons and cloth, and sit over tea or Arabic coffee in the evening. Falconry is a living tradition, and the falcon hospital close to the souq is an unexpected stop. The country hosted the football World Cup in 2022, and the city is still equipped with stadiums, a modern metro and wide new avenues.

Qatar is small, and so from Doha every ride is a short one. The roads are smooth, fast and well lit, with strict speed cameras on the highways and a firm attitude to the limit. The main routes run north toward the old pearl-trading town of Al Zubarah, a fortified settlement of the eighteenth century in the desert near the coast that is a World Heritage site, and south toward the dunes and the inland sea at Khor Al Adaid. Beyond the city, the land is stony desert, with little shade, ancient burial mounds, scrub and sometimes camels at the roadside. Sand blows across the surface in windy weather and can be treacherous on a motorcycle.

Summer is extremely hot and humid, with temperatures above forty degrees, so rides then are for sunrise only. From November to March the weather is mild and ideal. Fuel is cheap and stations are on every main road, with air-conditioned shops, and you can ride a long way before needing a refill. Coffee with dates in the souq is the habitual end to the evening.
t.coroico@-16.2,-67.7:
Coroico hangs on a green ridge in the Yungas, the steep, cloud-wrapped country where the Bolivian Andes fall away toward the Amazon basin. The town sits at about 1,700 metres, which is warm and humid after the thin air of La Paz, and the whole landscape smells of wet earth, coffee and citrus. For a rider arriving from the capital, it is the end of one of the most famous roads in the world, a place where you can finally breathe, sit in the shade and watch the clouds roll up the valley.

The old road, begun in the 1930s with forced labour by Paraguayan prisoners captured in the Chaco War, drops from the pass at La Cumbre, near 4,650 metres, to the jungle in barely sixty kilometres. The best season is the dry months from May to September. In the wet, rain can turn the road to mud within minutes, and in either season you should start early, because the afternoon cloud brings poor visibility. Ride slowly, stay on the correct side, and enjoy the sound of water everywhere.

La Cumbre is the top of the world for most riders, a cold, windy pass at about 4,650 metres on the edge of the Altiplano, where the road from La Paz crests the mountains and begins a descent of more than three thousand metres to the tropical Yungas. The name simply means the summit. There is a small shrine, a few stalls and, on a clear day, a view of snow-capped peaks, including Huayna Potosi, glowing white to the north. La Paz, with over 800,000 people in its metropolitan area, lies behind you, and Coroico, a small town in the cloud forest, is far below at the bottom of the descent.

The air is thin at this altitude, and both bike and rider feel it. Engines lose power, and a rider may get a headache, so take things slowly, drink water and avoid exertion. Fuel is not sold at the summit, so fill up in La Paz or El Alto, though be aware that Bolivian fuel prices and rules for foreigners have shifted over the years. The weather is changeable, with biting cold, sudden hail and thick fog. A good jacket and gloves are essential, even at midday.

From the summit, the modern road drops quickly through rocky gorges and into dense green forest, with sweeping bends and good tarmac, while the older road, the infamous Yungas Road, branches off to the north. Nicknamed the Road of Death, it was declared the world's most dangerous road by the Inter-American Development Bank in 1995 because of the number of accidents, and it is a narrow, unpaved shelf cut into a cliff, with drops of hundreds of metres. Since a new road opened, traffic has fallen, and the old road is mostly used by mountain bikers and adventurous riders. Treat it with respect, and avoid it in wet or foggy weather.

The history of the area is rich. The Altiplano was home to the Tiwanaku civilisation long before the Incas, and the Aymara people who live here today speak a language that predates Spanish by centuries. The road itself was originally built in the 1930s, partly by Paraguayan prisoners captured in the Chaco War, which adds a sober note to the ride. Llamas and alpacas graze on the plateau, and condors sometimes soar overhead.

The descent changes the climate dramatically. Within an hour the dry, cold air gives way to warm, wet cloud forest, orchids and bromeliads, coffee and coca terraces, and waterfalls across the road. Pack layers you can add and remove, and keep a rain jacket handy.

Chatham sits at the elbow of Cape Cod, where the arm bends and the Atlantic comes right up to the doorstep, and it is the sort of village that makes a good case for starting a ride on a weekday morning. The main street is lined with shingled shops, cafes and a bandstand, the houses are grey cedar with white trim, and the harbour is full of working boats. About 1,400 people live here year-round, and West Chatham, a quiet neighbour, has about as many. It is a place for stocking up, grabbing a coffee and a pastry and getting your bearings.

The riding is Cape Cod at its gentlest. Roads wander among salt marshes, ponds and low, scrubby woods, with short straights, easy curves and views of water opening up between the trees. Surfaces are generally good, although summer traffic, bicycles and slow-moving vehicles are a constant, and the speed limits are low and enforced. Heading north up the coast toward Nauset and Wellfleet takes you along the outer beaches, where the road runs close to the dunes and the sea breeze is strong. September and early October are the best months, with warm water, soft light and fewer visitors, while July and August can be crowded.

Chatham's connection to the sea is serious. The Chatham Light, a white tower on the bluff above the beach, has guided ships for more than a century, and the Coast Guard station nearby has performed daring rescues in the shoals offshore, where shifting sandbars have wrecked countless vessels. Down at the Fish Pier, you can watch commercial fishing boats unload their catch, and gulls and seals gather in the hope of scraps. In summer, the town holds Friday evening concerts in the park, a tradition that draws families with folding chairs and ice cream.

Offshore lies Monomoy, a long sandy barrier island that is a national wildlife refuge, home to enormous numbers of shorebirds and grey seals. Boat trips run out to see them, and the seals, which have returned in large numbers in recent decades, have in turn attracted great white sharks, a fact the town handles with a mixture of caution and fascination. The shoreline has changed repeatedly as storms break through the beach and reshape the harbour, and local people keep a close eye on it.

The air smells of salt marsh, pine and fried clams. Fuel is available in town, so top up before you set off, and carry a light jacket for the sea air.

Tambo Quemado is a border post on a road that runs across the roof of the Andes, and it is more a place you pass through than a place you visit. It sits at about 4,600 metres on the frontier between Bolivia and Chile, on the highway that links La Paz with the Pacific port of Arica. On the Chilean side the post is called Chungará, named after the nearby lake, and the customs sheds, trucks and little food stalls make up most of the scene. The air is thin and cold, and the wind blows constantly.

What makes it special is the setting. To the south rise the twin cones of Parinacota and Pomerape, snow-capped volcanoes of around 6,300 metres, and to the north, in Bolivia, stands Sajama, at 6,542 metres the highest peak in the country. They are among the most photogenic mountains in the Andes, with their reflections trembling in the lake on a calm morning. Chungará Lake, at some 4,500 metres, is one of the highest in the world, and its shores hold flamingos, giant coots and flocks of vicuñas.

Sajama National Park, established in 1939, is Bolivia's oldest, and it protects a high plateau of grassland, hot springs and geysers. The park has some of the highest forests on Earth, groves of queñua trees growing at over 5,000 metres, and herds of llamas and alpacas graze on the bofedales, boggy meadows, green in a brown landscape. Aymara herders live in small villages here, and a few stone houses and a colonial church add to the sense of a long human history.

The road is paved on both sides, which is a mercy, but the altitude is demanding: engines lose power, and a rider can get headaches or worse if they come up too quickly from the coast. Spend a night at middle height before crossing, drink water, and go slowly. Fuel is a real problem in this region, so fill the tank wherever you can before you get here and carry extra if you are able. Queues of trucks at the border can stretch for hours, and paperwork for foreign vehicles takes time, so start early, bring your documents and be patient. The best view of the volcanoes comes at dawn, when the light turns them pink.
t.north yungas road point 2@-16.3,-68.0:
La Cumbre is the high point of the North Yungas Road, a pass at roughly 4,650 metres above sea level where the road tips over the rim of the altiplano and heads down into the cloud forest. The setting is stark: cold, bare, boulder-strewn slopes with patches of snow, a few shrines and a statue of the Virgin, and a lot of wind. On a clear day the snow peaks of the Cordillera Real line up to the north, and the contrast with the green world below is almost theatrical.

There are no services at the pass itself, and La Paz is about twenty-two kilometres back, so make sure the tank is comfortable. The temperature can be near freezing even in the dry season, and fog and sleet are common. Many riders stop here for a moment to rest, add a layer for the descent, and take a photograph at the sign. Breathe slowly, because at this height even small efforts leave you winded, and be ready for a headache.

The old road, famous as the most dangerous in the world, starts a little below and was built in the 1930s, partly by Paraguayan prisoners of war captured during the Chaco War. Narrow, unpaved and bordered by drops of hundreds of metres, it claimed many lives in its heyday, and crosses in places mark where vehicles went over. A new paved highway now carries most traffic, so the old route is used mainly by cyclists and adventurous riders.

If you choose it, expect a steep, loose, wet and sometimes foggy gravel road with waterfalls pouring across the track. Drive on the left of the road, as local custom has it, so the driver can see the edge. Take it slowly, avoid riding in rain if you can, and carry water, tools and a spare tube. If you take the paved road instead, you still get dramatic views and a spectacular descent through cloud. Either way, this is one of the wonders of the continent.
